#6459. The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites

Massive galaxies like the Milky Way have a retinue of smaller, dim satellites on their outskirts. They're hard to detect, and while astronomers have found about 65 of the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies, and about 40 globular clusters in its halo, they suspect there are many dwarf satellites and globular clusters yet to be found. Now the Vera Rubin Observatory has found two more.

The Milky Way's satellites are either small dim galaxies or globular clusters, and both are part of the assembly history of the Milky Way through mergers. These two detections by the Rubin, found in its Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2) released in July 2026, are almost certainly the beginning of many more discoveries of Milky Way satellites by the powerful observatory. One is a most likely a dim dwarf galaxy named Aquarius IV, and one is a globular cluster named Rubin-GC1.

This figure shows the locations of both Rubin-GC1 and Aquarius IV. Rubin-GC1's detection was particularly impressive, since it's in the direction of the Milky Way's bulge, a region with a dense stellar population and thick dust. Image Credit: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA, ESA/Gaia/DPAC, W. Cerny

The discoveries are presented in two new papers.

One is titled "Discovery of the Distant, Ultra-faint Milky Way Satellite Aquarius IV with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2." It's published in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society, and the lead author is William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yaleâs Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

"We present the discovery of Aquarius IV (RubinâJ2201â0234)âthe first ultra-faint Milky Way (MW) satellite to be identified using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory," the authors write. It was confirmed in images from the Dark Energy Camera. The authors say it's a low-luminosity, compact stellar system in the outer Galactic halo.

It's stellar population is ancient and low-metallicity. "These properties closely resemble those of the smallest and faintest confirmed ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), though a globular cluster classification is not ruled out," the researchers write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies can have as little as a few hundred stars, which makes them smaller than some globular clusters (GCs). But there's one critical difference between UFDs and GCs: UFDs have dark matter while GCs don't (except for a few possible outliers).

Only a small number of the stars in Aquarius IV have been detected so far, so whether or not it is a UFD for sure will depend on deeper imaging and spectroscopy.

âWhat I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin,â said first author Cerny. (He is also the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.)

âIf the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries,â Cerny said. âThese new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter.â

These panels are images centered on Aquarius IV. The star in the lower panel marks a Blue Horizontal Branch star used to determine the distance to Aquarius IV. The stars in the bottom panel are also coloured according to their probability of being members of Aquarius IV. The grey stars are almost certainly not members, while colours ranging from purple through red, orange, and yellow represent increasing probability. Image Credit: William Cerny et al 2026 Res. Notes AAS 10 239

The second paper is "Rubin Observatory Reveals a Dust-Shrouded Halo Globular Cluster in Ophiuchus," and it will be published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. It's currently available at arxiv.org and the lead author is Aashay Pai. Pai is a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Chicago.

"We present the discovery of the Milky Way satellite Rubin-GC1 (Rubin J1628â1735) using data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatoryâs Early Data Preview 2," the authors write. The stars in Rubin-GC1 have an intermediate age of about 9.2 billion years, and are moderately rich in metals, meaning it's most likely a very faint GC. "Together, these properties suggest Rubin-GC1 is most likely a star cluster in the faint tail of the luminosity function of globular clusters surrounding the Milky Way," the authors write.

Based on comparisons to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Rubin-GC1 is most likely a cluster accreted to the Milky Way, associated with the Sagittarius leading arm. The Sagittarius leading arm is a massive tidal stream of stars from the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, torn away as that galaxy merges with the Milky Way.

The panel on the left shows the Sagittarius trailing and leading arms. (The DES images are not part of this work.) The image on the right shows roughly where Rubin-GC1 is located, shown with the gold star. The Milky Way's center is shown with the black cross, and the circle with the dot inside is the Sun. Image Credit: Left: By NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=139367207. Right: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âFinding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,â said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. âIt is remarkable this is now a reality.â

Rubin-GC1 was detected in the direction of the galactic bulge, where stellar density is very high and the dust is thick. Finding it in those conditions makes the detection even more impressive. "The discovery of Rubin-GC1 highlights the potential of Rubin to uncover faint, resolved satellites in dust-shrouded regions of the Milky Way, including remnants of the accretion events that have shaped the Galaxyâs hierarchical assembly," the authors write.

The panel on the left is what's called a 'smoothed isochrone filtered stellar density map.' It's a visualization tool in astronomy used to detect and map faint structures like ultra-faint dwarf galaxies by masking out field stars based on a color-magnitude curve. The panel on the right is a more familiar type of image used to show the region itself. Image Credit: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âThese discoveries are incredibly promising,â Geha said. âContinued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form.â

The Vera Rubin Observatory is mostly known as a transient-detecting observatory, and as the maker of a ten-year long movie of the sky in its Legacy Survey of Space and Time. But it's more than that. As it images the sky repeatedly, dim objects will become clearer. "The sensitivity of Rubin LSST will steadily increase, and systems similar to Aquarius IV are ultimately expected to be detectable with >85% efficiency using the same search algorithm applied here," the authors of the first paper write.

Not only that, but its observations will work with observations from other observatories, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to detect even more objects. "The identification of Rubin-GC1 heralds an exciting era of discovery as Rubin, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pierce the shroud of Galactic dust to reveal faint satellites that were hitherto hidden by our Galaxy," the authors of the second paper write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and globular clusters are puzzle pieces in the history of the Milky Way's growth through mergers. The mergers are ongoing, as interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way show.

By finding more of the Milky Way satellites, a picture of all of these mergers, and the role dark matter plays, will become clearer. By mapping out these objects and the streams they're sometimes a part of, astronomers can detect where dark matter also concentrates in clumps. These dark matter sub-halos will show how our galaxy grew larger by consuming smaller galaxies with their own dark matter halos.

#6458. Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi

There’s plenty of creative dishes coming out of this West Village kitchen

You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each week. The whimsical, caviar-topped dish really encapsulates what the restaurant is trying to achieve: “We should have serious food, serious hospitality, but we shouldn’t take ourselves too seriously,” says managing partner Ahris Kim. Here’s how the Somssi kitchen preps to create the newly famous potato and plenty of other dishes before a night of service.

Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.

Watch the team at Somssi create creative dishes like a triple-potato bite and a show-stopping grilled tongue dish in this episode of Mise En Place.

#6457. America’s Next Catastrophic Industrial Disaster May Already Be Underway

As fiercer storms collide with an aging industrial system, a unique kind of catastrophe is becoming more commonplace—and no one, it seems, is fully prepared to stop it.

On August 24, 2020, as Tropical Storm Laura churned up fury and foam in the Gulf of Mexico, employees at BioLab Inc. were racing to fill the trailers backed into the loading docks of the chlorine plant, located just outside of Lake Charles, Louisiana, with pallets of woven sacks. Each sack was stuffed with 2,750 pounds of granulated trichloroisocyanuric acid—trichlor for short—a chemical used to kill algae and bacteria in swimming pools. Trichlor dissolved slowly when submerged in water, the employees had learned in their annual safety training, but became hot enough to explode when exposed to small amounts of it—say, a slow leak or shallow flood, the kind of damage that might happen in a coastal region during a Category 4 storm.

By the next day Laura was officially a hurricane, and about 825,000 pounds of trichlor had left the warehouse, bound for a BioLab facility in Conyers, Georgia. Employees waited for the last two trucks that would carry the remaining one million pounds of the hazardous chemical to higher ground. But those trucks never arrived.

The plant’s 111-person staff had been whittled down to a hurricane crew, nine workers assigned to monitor the facility on-site during a storm. They arrived around 5 p.m. and began slinging sandbags and securing loose items. As the majority of Calcasieu Parish residents sat in long lines of traffic pointing away from the coast, the crew heaved the remaining 500 tons of trichlor on top of triple-stacked pallets—the idea was to keep the trichlor dry if floodwater did infiltrate the building. Plus, they’d be around if anything went wrong during the storm.

But as the sun rose the following morning, the solemn TV meteorologists all said the same thing: The impacts of Hurricane Laura, which became the strongest hurricane to strike Southwest Louisiana since the U.S. started keeping official records in 1851, would be “unsurvivable.” By 9:30 a.m., BioLab management had directed the hurricane crew to lock up the facility and evacuate with the rest of their neighbors.

So no one was in the warehouse during the early morning hours of Thursday, August 27, when Laura’s vicious, 150-mile-per-hour winds plucked portions of the roof off the building. No one was there to hear the drops of rain pelting those woven sacks of pool chemicals, to hear the pellets inside begin to crackle and hiss. No one saw those first few licks of flame, the first gust of black, poisonous smoke that would soon darken the sky.

“It smelled like if you took a swimming pool of human hair and lit it on fire,” remembers John O’Donnell, who arrived in Lake Charles later that morning to check on his house after the storm had passed. “I’ll never be able to forget what that smell smelled like.”

O’Donnell’s own roof had been damaged, but now his more pressing concern was the curdling, cast-iron cloud of chlorine gas that hovered over the town. Once used as a weapon of terror during WWI, chlorine can cause an array of symptoms including vomiting, blisters, shortness of breath, and burning pain in the lungs, throat, nose, and eyes.

As O’Donnell’s eyes began to burn, a photojournalist covering the hurricane wandered into his driveway. “What is that?” the photojournalist asked, looking skyward.

“That’s why your phone is about to go off,” said 33-year-old O’Donnell, a disaster recovery strategist who grew up in Southwest Louisiana, a storm-battered region dotted with petrochemical plants and emergency sirens. Just then, the shelter-in-place alert O’Donnell predicted blared from their phones. But shelter where? Six months into the COVID-19 pandemic, lockdown mandates had eased, but congregating indoors was still a bad idea. Anyway, it was 80-something degrees, and there wasn’t a building for miles that had electricity or water.

O’Donnell got back in his car and headed “as far away . . . as possible,” he says, a challenge given the debris and downed trees that lay strewn across the roads. “That was a really scary moment for everybody.”

It was a terrifying scene—but not an isolated one. For decades, experts have warned about the looming threat of so-called Natech disasters—technological failures triggered by natural hazards. The 1972 flood that ruptured a West Virginia coal slurry impoundment, destroying 550 homes and killing 125 people. The 1994 Southern California earthquake that shattered an oil pipeline, sending nearly 200,000 gallons of crude oil into a nearby river. The 9.0 earthquake off the coast of Japan in 2011 that produced a rare, double-wave tsunami, causing a meltdown at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in what is now considered one of the world’s most destructive nuclear catastrophes and the most expensive disaster in modern history.

As climate change drives more extreme weather, the conditions that produce these cascading disasters are becoming more common. “There are few events that are only natural disasters now,” says Liesel Ritchie, PhD, a sociologist at Virginia Tech who studies their social impacts. “And the more technology advances, the more likely these tightly coupled systems are to fail.” Yet even as the risks grow, readiness has not kept pace. Experts like Ritchie say the country remains woefully unprepared. The focus is still on natural disasters, she says, “because Natech events seem to be so rare.”

But they may not be as rare as we think. And across the country, millions of people live and work near industrial facilities like the one in Lake Charles, often unaware how vulnerable they are.

In 1994, Pamela Sands Showalter, then a University of Toledo geographer, and the late Mary Fran Myers, a disaster researcher at the University of Colorado, wrote in the journal Risk Analysis that “the number of incidents where natural and technological disasters interact is rising while preparations, which recognize the complications inherent in such combined events, remain cursory.”

As evidence, these preeminent disaster scholars pointed to the results of a survey they had conducted of emergency management agencies in 20 states that revealed an emerging trend in the number of chemical, oil, and radiological releases caused by natural disasters during the preceding 10 years. The results also showed that few legislative bodies had even considered the risk, let alone addressed it.

“Natech” disasters, as Showalter and Myers first called them, were “a growing, but as yet unstudied problem.”

Three-plus decades later, not much has changed. The risk of Natech disasters continues to grow, while efforts to prevent or prepare for them have largely stalled.

Between 1990 and 2017, Natech events essentially doubled in the U.S. In 2017, Hurricane Harvey caused 46 chemical leaks and nearly 100 hazardous substance spills. In 2021, Winter Storm Uri created prolonged power and water outages in Texas that contributed to more than 246 deaths. And in 2023, the megafires that devastated the island of Maui were the deadly consequence of high winds and sparking power lines.

Meanwhile, there is still no single federal law or agency dedicated to mitigating the risk of Natech disasters. Instead, preparedness is implemented through a patchwork of institutions—FEMA, OSHA, and the EPA, to name a few—and regulations regarding things like workplace safety and hazardous substances.

Further, because the U.S. emergency management system is designed as a bottom-up structure, where local governments are first responders—and because each region of the country deals with its own unique climatic and industrial risks—Natech prevention and response are often passed down by default to the state, county, and municipal governments.

The problem with this protocol, according to Ritchie, is that “expertise is not as strong as it is at the federal level.” Neither is funding (few towns have the training, let alone the equipment, to deal with a toxic chemical release). Additionally, planning for emergencies tends to happen in silos, so that an agency tasked with clearing roads after a storm has little to no interaction with the folks who might respond to an oil spill. Industry managers and government officials, meanwhile, don’t often engage in sustained and transparent dialogue. The disconnect between institutions often hampers a coordinated response during a disaster, prolonging the event and worsening the danger.

The natural and technical components of the disaster, on the other hand, work in tandem to intensify their impact. And these are not simply concurrent disasters, says O’Donnell, who has since taken a role as community resilience officer at the Baton Rouge Area Foundation. “They’re compounding disasters.”

After Hurricane Laura, for example, a power outage caused by the storm prevented the electric water pumps in BioLab’s fire protection system from functioning, allowing the fire to spread. As emergency crews rushed to shut down the interstate and put out the blaze, that was time they were not assisting the 8,000 families whose homes were lost or destroyed during the Category 4 hurricane. A closed interstate further delayed utility companies from restoring electricity and water to the tens of thousands without it, now sweltering in the September heat. The chemical fire raged for a full 24 hours, preventing people who still had a home from returning to get started on recovery.

Delayed recovery, whether it’s the additional hours for mold to fester inside homes or the expense of extra nights in a hotel, is often especially burdensome for those who live where the risk for Natech disasters is the highest: heavily industrialized, economically disadvantaged cities like Lake Charles, where almost a quarter of the population lives in poverty. Residents in these places already suffer from higher-than-average rates of health issues, thanks to prolonged exposure to pollution, and possess fewer resources to get back on their feet in the aftermath of disasters.

Perhaps most insidiously, Natech events can fracture communities and damage trust in human institutions. While a natural disaster tends to inspire cooperation and widespread mutual support, “man-made” disasters create “a far more severe and long-lasting pattern of social, economic, cultural, and psychological impacts,” according to the late UC Santa Barbara environmental sociologist William Freudenburg, PhD. In the aftermath of a technological disaster, fear, uncertainty, blame, and division abound. What’s often missing is collective action.

In the months after the fire, area residents did not come together to demand accountability or remuneration, even though the ensuing investigation found that the company was aware its facility had not been built to withstand severe hurricane damage or rainwater infiltration, despite the known risks involved.

For better or worse, Lake Charles is “tied to this chemical industry,” says James Hiatt, a former refinery worker who founded For Better Bayou, a local environmental justice nonprofit. As many as 45 percent of the non-farm jobs in Calcasieu and Cameron Parishes are connected in some way to the area’s approximately 30 chemical plants or petroleum refineries, which together account for more than half of the local tax base. This dependence on the industry means residents can be reluctant to speak out against offending companies or even press for regulation that might prevent the next disaster.

“I wish I could tell you it woke people up,” O’Donnell says. Local environmental groups “made the usual noise,” but in November 2022, BioLab cut the ribbon on its brand-new trichlor production facility in Lake Charles, rebuilt where the old one had burned down.

Meanwhile, less than two years later, another BioLab facility would go up in flames.

On the afternoon of Sunday, September 29, 2024, Iffat Walker was driving east on Interstate 20 to her home in Conyers, Georgia, a city of about 20,000 people just outside of Atlanta. Traffic was unusually backed up, and she was inching along the highway. That’s when she noticed the thick black cloud looming over the horizon.

“You couldn’t tell what it was,” she says, “I thought maybe a car fire.” But as she crept closer to the smoke, a strong chemical smell wafted through her car. She quickly rolled the windows up, but her skin began to tingle. By the time she arrived home about 20 minutes later, angry welts had bloomed on her arms.

“I was alarmed because I was sitting in it for such a long time,” says Walker, a nonprofit director. “I’m panicking at this point.”

It wasn’t until she turned on the news that Walker learned a facility called BioLab, which produced and stored millions of pounds of trichlor, had caught fire that morning, releasing a plume of highly toxic chlorine gas over the Atlanta metropolitan area.

It was not the disaster Georgians had expected that week. Just four days earlier, Governor Brian Kemp had declared a state of emergency ahead of Hurricane Helene. Although Helene ended up dumping more than 10 inches of rain on Conyers in just two days, it seemed the area had avoided severe catastrophe; that would turn out not to be true.

In fact, according to an investigation by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board (CSB) released in May 2025, BioLab employees on fire-watch duty inside the facility during the storm had reported multiple roof leaks. And, according to the CSB report, while no rain fell the day before the fire, and the employee who called 911 the morning of the blaze claimed that water from a burst sprinkler had made contact with the pallets of trichlor, the same employee later stated, “I think that it could’ve been water off the ceiling.” (What caused the fire has never been determined; BioLab declined to be interviewed.)

By Sunday evening, the warehouse was destroyed, and the fire was largely extinguished. But the danger was far from over.

The next day, Madelyne Reese woke up at her home about five miles outside of Conyers, where she sleeps with the windows open, and smelled something funny. She assumed it was just the lingering odor of the bleach she had used to clean that weekend, but when she opened the back door to let her dog out, she says, “I got smacked in the face with it.”

It had been 24 hours since the fire at the BioLab facility had started, but Reese had received no indication of the airborne contaminant—no sirens, no text messages. While neighborhoods in the immediate vicinity had been evacuated Sunday morning, residents in the surrounding areas received a patchwork of messages; some were told to evacuate, others to shelter in place. Some, like Reese, didn’t receive an alert until Monday afternoon. On Tuesday, the shelter-in-place order that had been issued and lifted on Monday was implemented again, as the toxic plume shifted with the wind.

By then, conditions had turned “brutal,” says Reese, a human resources director. “The smog hit and you could not see a foot and a half in front of you.” On that hot, early autumn day, Reese turned off the air conditioning and ran masking tape down the seams of her windows. “I was just trapped in here. I’ve never experienced anything like it.” Four days later, Reese’s horse, a black Tennessee Walker she’d rescued from a kill pen, suddenly developed a cough and had trouble breathing.

In the aftermath of the fire, the roughly 15,000 students in the Rockdale County Public School District attended classes online, while businesses in the two-mile contamination zone remained shuttered. Monitoring stations showed chlorine levels up to 20 times the Environmental Protection Agency’s exposure guidelines. (A 2026 study by scientists at the Georgia Institute of Technology would show that the air also contained dangerously high levels of bromine and isocyanic acid, toxic chemicals that can cause lung problems as well as irritation of the eyes, nose, throat, and skin.) People in surrounding areas complained of headaches, rashes, and dizziness and watched their flowerbeds wither.

Yet information remained scarce. What caused the incident? What chemicals were in the air? Should residents wear masks? “Complete silence,” says Reese. “Our government wasn’t giving us any answers.” So Reese started a Facebook group called Stand Against BioLab in Rockdale County. “We all needed to talk, we all needed to figure it out,” she says. The group quickly swelled to over 1,500 members.

They learned that this BioLab facility had actually caught fire three times in the last two decades (earning it the nickname “Firelab” with emergency management personnel), and that the company, one of Rockdale County’s largest employers, had received generous tax breaks since it opened in 1973.

Other community groups coalesced and disseminated petitions and planned protests. Farmers came together to test for pollutants on their land. Walker’s nonprofit, Community Action NOW!, partnered with the Morehouse School of Medicine to launch a three-year study to track long-term health impacts resulting from the fire.

And collectively, these groups began to call for legal action—and for the facility to be shut down.

Their activism worked. Less than a month after the fire, Rockdale County officials filed a federal lawsuit seeking compensation for impacted residents and called for the company to leave Conyers.

While the county’s lawsuit was partially dismissed, including some demands for damages, that litigation is still active, as is a class action suit. And in May 2025, BioLab announced it had completed remediation of the site and would no longer produce trichlor in Conyers (though it would continue to store the chemical there).

“I’d like to think it was . . . how vocal we were as a community,” says Reese, who admits the experience has left her jaded. “But there are a million BioLabs out there that are not being held to true standards.”

Days after BioLab’s announcement, the CSB released its report, which revealed that on the morning of the fire, the facility had contained double the amount of trichlor the company had previously disclosed—including half a million pounds of the chemical that had been shipped from Lake Charles in 2024 as Hurricane Francine bore down on the Gulf Coast.

Following the investigation, OSHA proposed $61,473 in penalties against BioLab, whose parent company, KIK Custom Products, has reported estimated annual revenues of more than $2 billion. (The penalty was paid in full, according to a Department of Labor spokesperson, and the case is now closed.)

On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.0 undersea earthquake struck off Japan’s northeastern coast, triggering a massive tsunami that inundated the Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant, which sat on a 30-foot bluff overlooking the Pacific Ocean. While the reactors shut down safely, seawater flooded the plant’s backup generators. After days without cooling, three of the plant’s four reactor cores overheated and began to melt down, releasing lethal amounts of radiation into the atmosphere and ocean in the worst nuclear disaster since Chernobyl, the 1986 explosion at a Soviet power plant that displaced more than 200,000 people and caused long-term environmental contamination. Parts of the Daiichi area remain so radioactively hot that the robots sent in to assess the damage in 2017 were instantly fried.

A Japanese parliamentary panel later called the disaster “clearly man-made,” blaming systemic failures across every institution involved—the government, regulatory authorities, and the company that owned the plant.

They “betrayed the nation’s right to be safe from nuclear accidents,” the panel’s report said.

In the years since, Japan has taken an aggressive, wide-ranging approach to preventing similar disasters, including the creation of an independent watchdog agency to enforce regulations that explicitly require plants to consider extreme natural hazards and compounding disasters. Existing plants were required to install higher seawalls and more resilient backup power sources and must now continuously assess seismic and tsunami risks.

The country’s new policies aren’t built around the assumption that these disasters are possible, but rather that they are inevitable.

That is decidedly not the case in the U.S., where many of the agencies responsible for preventing, mitigating, or responding to Natech disasters are now being downsized or defunded. For example, the Trump Administration has canceled or delayed billions of dollars in FEMA grants meant to harden infrastructure against hurricanes, fires, and floods. Meanwhile, the EPA has shed a quarter of its workforce, including many staff who focused on environmental justice for disadvantaged communities dealing with the long-term impact of pollution, places like Lake Charles. The White House has even tried to eliminate the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, an independent body that investigates the causes of chemical releases and proposes ways accidents could be avoided. (Congress ultimately saved the agency.)

And then there are cuts to climate research that could inform future planning and policy pertaining to Natech disasters. In 2025, the Administration ordered NOAA to stop tracking extreme weather events that cause over $1 billion in damage and canceled National Science Foundation grants for more than 100 research projects on climate change.

This disinvestment is having an “adverse impact on . . . communities that need this information,” Virginia Tech’s Ritchie says. But she believes there are still things communities can do to protect themselves. Ritchie points out that major industrial projects (like a mine, a dam, or a large factory) involving federal permits or funding require review under the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act, a process that mandates an environmental impact evaluation. These assessments include an opportunity for public comment on potential socio-economic benefits and risks associated with a project, as well as what the community stands to lose in the event of a disaster or hazard. It doesn’t guarantee this input will be addressed, she says, but it can lead to negotiations between communities, developers, and governments over things like mitigation measures and compensation—not just financial restitution but programs that address quality of life, such as a new community center or coverage for mental health services.

On an individual level, being prepared can make all the difference, according to Madelyne Reese, who was unaware there was even a chemical plant near her home. “Understand who is operating in your city and your county,” she says. Invest in the appropriate PPE and develop an evacuation plan. “Don’t wait until it’s in your backyard.”

Four months after it reopened, the BioLab plant in Lake Charles once again experienced a chlorine leak. Then, in July 2024, another thick plume of smoke arose over the warehouse. Both incidents caused a temporary closure of I-10 and a shelter-in-place order. While environmental activists have called for the facility to be shut down, those voices remain in the minority.

Still, if you ask James Hiatt, who still remembers that August 2020 day when the wreckage of his city lay scattered beneath a roiling cloud of chlorine smoke, the subject of BioLab’s threat to the community “is never black and white; there’s a lot of gray.”

BioLab employs more than 100 residents and supports the county’s tax base, providing revenue for public schools and sheriffs’ departments. It donates money and volunteer hours to local nonprofits and community events, including school programs and field trips. And, argues Jim Rock, the executive director of the Lake Area Industrial Alliance—a coalition of refineries, liquid natural gas operators, and chemical manufacturers—the company has its own incentives for prioritizing safety. “They don’t want something bad to happen to them or their industrial neighbors,” he says, pointing to the improvements BioLab made when it opened the new facility in 2022—like elevated work floors and structures that can withstand 150mph winds. “I’m more confident in the integrity of facilities now . . . than I was 10 or 20 years ago,” he says.

Rock, who worked for decades in chemical plants, insists the industry is safe. “We’re constantly being audited by both state and federal inspectors to ensure that we’re doing everything we’re supposed to be doing,” he says. “Those rules don’t get lax over time. [The facilities are] historically safe places . . . because they have to be. You got to take extra precautions because you got extra hazards.”

As for the people who live near these operations, researchers have found that residents in disaster-prone areas often have little choice but to look on the bright side. “A chronic disaster is one that gathers force slowly and insidiously, creeping around one’s defenses rather than smashing through them,” wrote the late Yale University sociologist Kai Erikson in A New Species of Trouble, a seminal book that examines the unique and disruptive effects of human-caused disasters. “People are unable to mobilize their normal defenses against the threat, sometimes because they have elected consciously or subconsciously to ignore it, sometimes because they have been misinformed about it, and sometimes because they cannot do anything to avoid it in any case.”

Hiatt says that his neighbors’ ability to stay positive in the face of grave danger is both a shortcoming and a strength.

“We are resilient,” says Hiatt. But he doesn’t mince words when it comes to the path ahead. “If we don’t stop what we’ve been doing, take a different road, this place will not be here in 100 years.”

And when Hiatt says “we,” he doesn’t just mean the residents of Southwest Louisiana.

According to a 2025 UCLA study, more than 5,500 hazardous sites across the country are projected to be at risk of coastal flooding by the end of the century, including facilities that handle sewage, toxic waste, and oil and gas. In the Midwest, the Chicago area is experiencing a surge in tornadoes, a looming threat to the region’s high concentration of toxic waste sites and coal ash ponds. Residents of Appalachia, where abandoned coal mines dot the landscape, see more frequent and intense flooding events than ever.

The few Americans lucky enough to live far from industrial facilities still rely on them for their everyday lives. For example, BioLab is one of the country’s largest producers of the chlorine used in pools and spas. Other Southwest Louisiana plants, meanwhile, churn out the building blocks for essential products like plastics, fertilizers, clothing, medical supplies, and electronics. The state’s 15 oil refineries account for about one-sixth of the U.S.’s refining capacity; its natural gas heats homes all over the country.

“We’re all part of a system that’s causing . . . harm,” says Hiatt. “We don’t have to align politically to see we’re interconnected and inter- dependent.”

Natech disasters are an existential threat. If we want to prevent them, he says, we have to begin by recognizing and acknowledging who’s at risk: all of us.

#6456. Stubborn Asteroids Around White Dwarfs Resist Becoming Dust

White dwarfs are the remnants of a stars like our Sun. For their sizeâthey're roughly the size of Earthâthey're extremely dense, and have about as much mass as the Sun. That means they have enormous gravitational power, enough power to tear apart objects that get too close.

For a long time, white dwarfs appeared to be alone in space, not including any stellar companions. Then observations showed that some of their surfaces were polluted with metals. Astronomers surmised that these metals were raining down onto their surfaces from rocky debris. Then came observations that some white dwarfs were surrounded by debris disks. After that, even more piercing observations found evidence of rocky bodies in the disks: small planets, moons, or asteroids.

An example of these is WD 1145+017, which seems to be orbited by several small rocky bodies, being torn apart and raining debris down onto the white dwarf's surface.

Scientists are curious about this process and how effectively white dwarfs can shred smaller bodies and form debris disks. As they find white dwarfs with disks, asteroids, and even planetary systems, explanations need to keep pace.

In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, researchers examined how efficiently white dwarf tidal forces can break asteroids apart. The research is titled "Size Limits on Tidal Debris around White Dwarfs: The Kilometer-size Barrier." The lead author is Jordan K. Steckloff, senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute.

"Compact disks of planetary debris orbiting white dwarfs provide a crucial window into our understanding of evolved planetary systems," the authors write. "The formation of these disks has been widely modeled with tidal fragmentation of minor planets that are rubble piles with no internal strength."

This artist's illustration shows a white dwarf surrounded by a debris disk, with asteroidal fragments in the foreground. The more astronomers find white dwarfs with debris disks, the more they want to understand how they're created. Image Credit: NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center/Scott Wiessinger

That's a problem because real rubble piles have some cohesive strength. Also, all three of the asteroids we've sampledâItokawa, Ryugu, and Bennuâare rubble piles. The force that holds these types of asteroids together is called the Van der Waals force. It's a weak, short-range force that attracts and repulses atoms and molecules. But as gecko feet show, it can be very effective.

In their work, Steckloff and his co-authors show what happens when this strength is included in modelling: "breakup of these rubble piles sets a maximum fragment size, and we calculate this size for water ice, iron, and material densities corresponding to the lunar highlands, Vesta, and the Earth," they write.

âNothing is truly strengthless,â Steckloff said. âTiny attractions between grains called Van der Waals forces give comets and asteroids a minimum strength 10 to 100 times weaker than pulling apart freshly fallen snow.â

According to this research, the typical internal strength of a rubble pile is â¼10â1000 Pa, which is about one million times weaker than solid rock. In that range, the maximum size for fragments is about the same as small asteroids, between about 0.1 and 1 km in diameter. "This limitâthe kilometer-size barrierâalso represents the characteristic sizes of tidal fragments," the authors explain. "Most of the debris mass is contained in fragments of this size."

These panels show characteristic debris size by distance from a white dwarf with about 0.6 solar masses and cohesive strength. The panel on the left is for a strength of 10 pascals, and the panel on the right is for a strength of 1 kilopascal. The results show characteristic fragment sizes of about 100 meters and 1,000 meters respectively. Image Credit: Jordan K. Steckloff et al 2026 ApJL 1004 L27

The authors say that as a consquence, models of disk formation around white dwarfs need to include another dust-generating factor in order to explain the dusty disks in observations. That likely means collisions rather than tidal forces.

The force that shapes the end-state of the disk is called PoyntingâRobertson drag. It explains how solar radiation affects dust grains around stars, including white dwarfs, making the dust spiral inward. This only works if the dust grains are small enough to be subjected to the drag but not so large that radiation pressure drives them away. This work shows that fragmentation itself isn't enough to create dust this small.

Observations in our Solar System agree with these results. When the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 approached Jupiter in 1992, the gas giant's powerful tidal force pulled the comet apart. But not into dust; instead, the comet was torn into fragments 100m to 1,000m in diameter, which then plunged into the planet.

This Hubble Space Telescope image shows comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broken into fragments after it approached Jupiter in 1992. Two years later the fragments approached Jupiter again and plunged into its atmosphere. Image Credit: NASA.

The research extends beyond asteroid fragment sizes in disks. It also shows that fragments maintain their orbits. They experience only tiny, fractional changes in their velocities "on the order of one part per million to one part per 100 million," the authors explain. "Such tiny changes in speed result in negligible changes to the orbits of the fragments, which remain in practically the same orbit as prior to disruption."

There are a lot of factors involved in the creation of a white dwarf's dust disk, and this work places an important constraint on one of them. "Understanding the progression from an intact minor planet to a sea of dust that is accreted onto a white dwarf is an outstanding challenge," the authors write. "In this Letter, we demonstrate a sharp constraint on the first step of this process." The work shows that some type of grinding process like collisions is required to generate white dwarf dust disks.

âUnderstanding the details of how debris around white dwarfs is produced and evolves is important for putting the observations into context,â said study co-author Kat Volk from the Planetary Science Institute. âThis will help us understand what happens to the small bodies in orbit around a star as it undergoes the end stages of its life.â

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6454. How Flavored Syrup Became a Coffee-Shop Culture War

For some coffee shop customers, premade syrups are now a major red flag. It presents a new opportunity for small business owners.

In a TikTok video with over 82,000 likes, the person behind the camera zooms into the shelves at a Pennsylvania coffee shop, three rows stacked with an array of Torani syrups in flavors like blueberry, brown-sugar cinnamon, English toffee, and salted caramel. “I just know my latte isn’t going to be good,” the caption reads. Across social media, similar sentiments appear. “If I see these at a cafe, I’m walking out immediately,” says one tweet, co-signed by many commenters. In a multipart video series, another creator documents her journey of replacing all of her Torani syrups with ones from small businesses instead. Last year, the niche food newsletter Unsnackable published what was described as a “Torani tirade.”

It’s not just a Torani problem, though the brand — by virtue of its market dominance — tends to get the most flack on social media. While some people seem to prefer competitor Monin, it, too, draws backlash over allegations of tasting “like chemicals.” The problem, for some drinkers of dessert-like specialty beverages, is premade syrups across the board.

For a certain sect of consumers, they’ve become a coffee shop red flag, a sign that a so-called “specialty” establishment asking them to fork over $8 plus tip for a latte is unfairly cutting corners when it comes to quality or craft. For these consumers, mass-market syrups now symbolize exactly that: They’re synonymous with coffee chains and corporations, the kind of impersonal institutions that many people are trying to get away from when they patronize a small business. The flip side: For independently owned coffee shops across the country, house-made syrup now represents a major opportunity.

When Carrie and Dennis Medina first envisioned their coffee shop, Room Service, in Ventura, California, they thought they would take an approach similar to the one at Sightglass Coffee, where they’d both gotten their start. “Very purist, with no syrups, no specialty drinks,” Dennis says. They imagined eight kinds of pour-over coffee and an emphasis on single-origin beans, since the couple also runs a roastery. “We said we’re never gonna do cream tops; we’re never gonna do these crazy drinks,” Carrie says. But in the first week alone, every customer was asking for them.

Now, Room Service offers 10 to 12 different syrups at any given time (and six different cream tops), all of them made in-house. It offers drinks such as a cinnamon roll latte topped with a cinnamon roll, and a honey cornbread latte with an ube cream top. “I hear that question all the time,” Dennis says. “‘Hey, do you guys make your syrups in-house?’” To him, a shop that isn’t trying to do at least the basics — like vanilla — in-house is “falling behind what the times are pushing for.”

The demand for syrups and other embellishments is so intense that the Medinas have brought on a full-time prep person who works exclusively on “all these things that we do in-house that make us special,” Carrie says. Room Service’s PSL, for example, starts with kabocha squash. It’s roasted, blended with spices such as cloves and cinnamon, and cooked into syrup, a process that takes two days. Echoing a sentiment that seems common among coffee shop owners right now, Carrie describes their current approach as “not necessarily the coffee shop we wanted, but it’s more like the coffee shop we have to be.” And if the market demands syrups and cream tops, then the Medinas wanted to ensure that the intention and emphasis on quality that they applied to their coffee beans also carried over.

In 2025, Michael Smith opened Trust Coffee Co. in Bay Village, Ohio, taking over, remodeling, and rebranding an older coffee shop. He, like the Medinas, imagined a more “pour-over, third-wave” style establishment. “But I’ve been a business owner for a long time,” says Smith, who also runs a restaurant and a catering business. “I’ve realized over the years that your customers tell you more about who you are than who you actually think you are.” His customers, it turned out, wanted seasonal syrups in niche flavors like maple rosemary, caramelized banana, and strawberry rhubarb.

The purist is no longer coffee’s north star; the maximalist is.

Syrups like Monin, which the shop’s previous iteration used, “serve a purpose in the industry,” Smith says, but he wanted more control over the menu. The two full-time pastry chefs from Smith’s other businesses oversee the shop’s syrups. “It’s become such a huge thing,” he says: Every time Trust’s social media manager posts a new syrup, the line is out the door for a week. “It sets us apart,” he explains.

When Sabrina Kaylor opened the first location of Bizarre Coffee in Canton, Georgia in 2020, the shop used bottled syrups. She hadn’t worked in coffee prior, and she said that approach felt like the norm at the time. “It allowed us to hone our craft and learn what we were doing,” she says. Over time, Kaylor — who’s quite active on the company’s official social media platforms — noticed that the tenor of the conversation was changing: In the immediate post-COVID years, people were making more things at home and there was more pride to be gained in “scratch-made.” With her business becoming known for lattes in flavors such as blueberry, banana, and guava, Kaylor decided to shift toward more house-made syrups. Previously, her customers didn’t ask about their sourcing, but now, they ask all the time.

As much as there is a sense of valor in the entirely from-scratch approach, Kaylor retains some skepticism about the current torrent of Torani and Monin backlash. Today, 90 percent of Bizarre’s drinks use house-made syrups, though one of its best-selling drinks still relies on the bottled stuff; Bizarre’s menu is extensive and making everything in-house would be a significant investment of labor. On the part of coffee shops, “I think a lot of [the house-made syrup conversation] is marketing, quite honestly,” Kaylor says. As for the bandwagoning that is all the anti-Torani memes, “I think it’s part of consumer behavior,” she says. And that, she acknowledges, can be really “discouraging” for small business owners.

In a sense, that’s what the premade-versus-house-made-syrup conversation boils down to: the stand between small businesses and big ones. For more consumers, the economic and social conditions of the current moment have inspired increased skepticism toward the influence of corporations and private equity in the food and beverage world.

The Minnesota coffee shop Little Joy has become famous across social media for posting the recipes of its signature drinks in detailed DIY videos. It has since launched a membership program through which other coffee shop owners can purchase its recipes, scaled up for commercial usage; gain access to training videos; and sell its drinks without even needing to attribute them to Little Joy, though the ones that would like to can pin their use of Little Joy’s recipes to a Drink Finder map.

Yes, these might just be recipes for syrups and foams, but in an interview with Eater’s industry newsletter Pre Shift earlier this year, Little Joy owner Cody Larson described the system as a way to build solidarity among independent businesses. “The big coffee chains, they’re never gonna do house-made syrups, so I think that’s where independent shops can get a leg up,” he said. “Ultimately, the chains are our competition... If independent shops can, in any way possible, raise the bar across the board, that’s good for all independent shops, including us.”

It’s hard to look at the drinks coming out of specialty coffee shops today — fluffy with foam, flavored to emulate nuanced desserts like princess cake and tiramisu— and not think of the Starbucks Frappuccino. The combination of app-ordering and social media “hack” culture have mainstreamed super-elaborate beverage requests, allowing Starbucks and coffee chains like it to become purveyors of highly complicated customizable beverages, mainstreaming the mindset of the aforementioned “hyperflavor.”

When it comes to why consumers have moved away from the single-origin pour-over approach at shops like his, “my guess is that these are a lot of people who used to be Starbucks loyalists and they’re looking for something that’s more local,” Smith says. “It’s a trend across everything where people want local, and we’re able to provide what Starbucks did, but in a more high-quality, more local way.”

Intentionality is what people are gravitating towards, especially as prices rise. If consumers are spending so much on a drink that’s undeniably a luxury, then they want to know that every part of that drink has been made carefully. And if they’re going to make the trip to a new, independent shop, they want to know that the offerings there aren’t the ones they can get anywhere, made with easily attainable, big-brand flavorings. For small coffee shops, the key to success could be as simple as syrup.

#6453. What Will Politics Look Like on Other Planets? It's Likely to Be a Mishmash

When we make our home on other worlds, who will be in charge?

Will it be an emperor, like the main character in âDune: Part Three,â the final movie in a trilogy based on Frank Herbertâs sci-fi saga? Or a billionaire, like the space mogul who plays a key role in setting up a Mars base in âFor All Mankindâ? Or a rebel alliance, like the revolutionaries in âStar Warsâ and âThe Moon Is a Harsh Mistressâ?

Jacob Haqq Misra, an astrobiologist who literally wrote the book on space sovereignty, suggests that itâll be none of the above, at least during the initial phases of extraterrestrial expansion.

âYouâre going to have Earth cultures represented, and ideas about Earth governance represented, and what will emerge is sort of a mishmash legal framework of agreements for how to coexist peacefully,â he says in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast. âThatâs maybe not even so bad.â

During our podcast chat, Misra laid out what sounds like a sensible perspective on the future of space politics, based on earthly precedents rather than starry-eyed assumptions about the final frontier.

For more than a decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk has talked up the prospect of building a city on Mars â and more recently, a base on the moon. But who would be in charge? Thatâs an open question even for Musk, who joked at a 2016 tech conference about being declared âking of Mars.â In a more serious vein, he said the future form of Martian government was likely to be âa direct democracy, not representative.â

âIt would be people voting directly on issues,â Musk said. âAnd I think thatâs probably better because the potential for corruption is substantially diminished in a direct vs. a representative democracy.â

Musk also had some novel ideas about the legislative process.

âIt should probably be easier to remove a law than create one,â he said. âI think thatâs probably good because laws have infinite life unless theyâre taken away. So, I think my recommendation would be something like, letâs say, 60% of people need to vote in a law, but at any point greater than 40% of people can remove it. And any law should come with a built-in sunset provision. If itâs not good enough to be voted back in, maybe it shouldnât be there.â

Misra, who is the chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space, explains in detail why it wouldnât be that easy to create a Martian government in a book titled âSovereign Mars.â The reason has to do with the Outer Space Treaty, a nearly 60-year-old agreement signed by more than 110 nations, including the United States, China, Russia and all the other space powers.

The treaty declares that all nations have the right to use the moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes, but also says no nation can claim sovereignty or ownership of extraterrestrial territory. Moreover, governments bear responsibility and legal liability for their national space activities, whether carried out by public agencies or private ventures. Which means the treaty would keep Elon Musk from being the king of Mars, even if SpaceX builds its own city.

At least thatâs the way Misra sees it. Robert Zubrin, the president of the nonprofit Mars Society, sees it differently. In his view, the treatyâs provisions mean the signatories âhave explicitly signed away their rights to interfere with Mars settlement.â But how long would it take for a Mars settlement to stand on its own, without governmental assistance?

âThere are a lot of challenges to living on Mars that make it more difficult,â Misra says. âAnd thatâs what I think is valuable about thinking about governance on Mars: not that itâs a place to start over, but itâs a way to challenge our ideas to the extreme. Maybe we never live on Mars full time, but we challenge our ideas and apply those back here on Earth.â

Misra sees plenty of earthly parallels to the sorts of issues raised by the prospect of space settlement, and they get the full treatment in âSovereign Mars.â

The author of âSovereign Marsâ is Jacob Haqq Misra, chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space. (Book cover design by Karl Janssen; Mars photo via NASA / JPL-Caltech / ASU / MSSS; author photo courtesy of Jacob Haqq Misra)

For example, consider the Antarctic Treaty System, which was set up nearly 70 years ago. The 58-nation treaty puts a freeze (heh, heh) on territorial claims of sovereignty. Administrative decisions about international activities in Antarctica are made by a 29-nation grouping of consultative parties, assisted by a secretariat based in Argentina.

Will Antarctica become independent? Misra doesnât think so â and he thinks the same line of reasoning would apply to Mars, at least in the early days of Red Planet exploration and settlement.

âTo imagine a city of a million people on Mars â Iâm not saying it wonât happen, but itâs very difficult to do so,â Misra says. âWe donât have cities that big on Antarctica. There doesnât really seem to be an economically compelling reason for it, although thereâs a lot of science on Antarctica. â¦ So, the lesson from reality and from science fiction is: Donât forget that itâs really, really hard to live in these harsh places.â

The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea serves as another instructive example. That treaty lays out principles for coordinating activities in the worldâs oceans â including the establishment of exclusive economic zones that extend 200 nautical miles beyond a nationâs territorial waters. Within those zones, each nation holds sovereign rights to resource extraction, energy production and research while still allowing for free navigation and overflight.

Even though the United States never ratified the Law of the Sea Treaty, it follows many of the treatyâs provisions due to pragmatic considerations. Misra thinks a similar sense of pragmatism will guide the settlement process on the moon and Mars.

For example, if the United States and China both establish bases at the moonâs south pole, they could agree to establish exclusive economic zones surrounding those settlements.

âI donât expect territorial conflict,â Misra says. âThe moon is really big. Itâs going to be a while before we run into the problem of two entities wanting to occupy the same place. I donât know of any regions of the moon that are so desirable that only one actor, one space agency, could get there to the exclusion of others.â

But Misra doesnât think thereâll be a new treaty to formalize a space governance system, or a new international authority along the lines of the United Earth Space Probe Agency in the fictional âStar Trekâ universe. The United Nations tried unsuccessfully to go down that road in 1979 with an international pact known as the Moon Treaty.

âItâs on the books,â Misra says. âIt has a number of signatories, but a very small number of signatories, none of which actually have their own independent launch capabilities. And so, many legal scholars consider it a dead treaty.â

Instead, Misra suspects that the worldâs space powers will find ways to âcooperate in space in a way that preserves their joint sovereignty.â

âI think there will be new multi-actor consortiums that have relevance,â he says. âThey might be outside the jurisdiction of the United Nations, for example, but they might be great things that arenât just driving forward profits for private entities. They might really reflect cooperation for science and exploration.â

What might that look like on the moon and Mars?

âProbably what would be likely is something similar to maybe a hybrid of Antarctic settlements and the way the International Space Station works,â Misra says. âIn Antarctica, there are various distances between the different outposts. Some might be closer than others, and each countryâs laws apply to that module,â he says.

The arrangements on the International Space Station are even more complicated, because each module hooked up to the outpost is the property of the nation that built the module. âYou get these weird agreements where, when data is transmitted from one section to the other, itâs actually governed by several different nationsâ laws along the way,â Misra says. âAnd if you are a Russian and you move down a couple of modules, youâre now a Russian visiting America.â

Thatâs likely to lead to a Martian mishmash. âI think you have to accept some degree of pluralism with what comes on Mars,â Misra says.

But does that mean space settlements will always be a mishmash? Not necessarily. There could be several ways to get around the Outer Space Treatyâs barriers to sovereignty. For example, an ambitious spacefaring nation could simply withdraw from the treaty, and then assert full sovereignty over the territory it controls. In 2011, space billionaire Robert Bigelow warned that China might do exactly that.

Another option would be for a company like SpaceX to move its base of operations (including its launch facilities) from the U.S. to a country that isnât a party to the Outer Space Treaty.

In âSovereign Mars,â Misra suggests a different route to extraterrestrial independence. The U.S. government, for example, could pass a law surrendering its territorial claim to an area under its control on the moon or Mars.

âIf you get the blessing from Congress, then youâve got the backing of a nation-state that says we agree with this long-term vision of establishing autonomy,â he says. âThere might be a discussion about it at the U.N., but you know, if I had to guess, if the United States did that, weâd hear about China doing something similar in a few years.â

When it comes to determining the long-term future of Martian governance, Misra actually agrees with Musk.

âWhat I think is, the Martians should decide,â Misra says. âIâm interested to see what they would think works, because it might be different models than what we come up with on Earth, simply because living on Mars is different than living anywhere here.â

More from Jacob Haqq Misra on space sovereignty:

In addition to his work as an astrobiologist and an expert on space sovereignty, Jacob Haqq Misra delves into the mysteries surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena, or UAP. He is a member of the UAP Science Advisory Council and the lead author of a study suggesting that a group of six small objects seen in a video recorded from a military aircraft near Kuwait was a flock of birds. Misra is also on the editorial review board for Limina â The Journal of UAP Studies and one of the editors of a forthcoming book titled âThe Politics of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Science, Security and Society.â

âDune: Part Threeâ opens in U.S. theaters on Dec. 18.

#6451. Something Remarkable Is Happening to Dogs Living Near Chernobyl’s Nuclear Plant

Scientists studying wild dogs near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have uncovered unusual genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than radiation-induced mutations.

Dogs living near the Chornobyl (previously called Chernobyl) Nuclear Power Plant carry genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than mutations caused by radiation exposure. A new genomic analysis identified more than 100 locations in their DNA showing signs of directional selection, including regions associated with DNA repair, cancer development, and immune function.

The findings suggest that environmental pressures may have favored certain inherited genetic variants, potentially helping some dogs survive in a contaminated environment. However, researchers have not established whether radiation or other environmental hazards directly caused these patterns.

Earlier research revealed substantial genetic differences between dogs living at the nuclear power plant and those in Chornobyl City, just 10 miles away. City dogs closely resembled populations from Russia, Poland, and surrounding regions, while dogs near the plant had distinctive genetic features, particularly in areas associated with DNA repair.

“This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population’s genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren’t due to mutation,” said Megan Dillon, postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.

“With this work, we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers – are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?”

Natural selection occurs when inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common across generations. Directional selection is a form of this process in which particular traits become increasingly favored, often in response to environmental conditions. Genetic drift, by contrast, involves random changes in the frequency of genetic variants. It can have especially strong effects in small, isolated populations and may reduce genetic diversity over time.

To distinguish between these processes, researchers compared the two Chornobyl dog populations with free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and an isolated population from the Galápagos Islands. This allowed them to examine whether geographic isolation alone could explain the unusual genetic patterns near the nuclear plant.

Although the plant dogs had a small effective population size, a measure of how many individuals contribute genetically to future generations, it was not significantly different from that of the city dogs. The plant population also lacked the reduction in genetic diversity expected from substantial genetic drift. Moreover, its genetic makeup differed markedly from other isolated populations, including the Galápagos dogs. Surprisingly, the Chornobyl City dogs were genetically more similar to the Galápagos population than to the dogs living at the nearby nuclear facility.

The researchers found evidence consistent with directional selection in genomic regions containing genes involved in DNA replication and repair, cell cycle regulation, cancer-related processes, and immune responses. These biological functions could influence how animals respond to harmful environmental exposures, although the analysis cannot determine whether particular variants actually improve survival.

“While we can’t say for certain whether what we’ve found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection,” Dillon said.

“When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment.”

The genetic differences do not necessarily mean that dogs developed new adaptations after exposure to radioactive contamination. Another possibility is that individuals carrying advantageous genetic variants were more likely to survive earlier environmental pressures, allowing those variants to become more prevalent in subsequent generations.

“When we consider the toxic environment around Chornobyl, I can see why most people would think, ‘Surely there’s got to have been some consequence of living in that environment,’” said Matthew Breen, Oscar J. Fletcher Distinguished Professor of Comparative Oncology Genetics at NC State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and corresponding author of the study.

“But what we’re saying is the consequence may not have gone as far as changing the dogs’ genome in order to adapt, it could be the ones that were able to survive the initial exposures had this level of underlying genetic diversity and variants to offer a higher degree of fitness,” Breen added. “Obviously that’s speculation, and we don’t know exactly what’s happened. But it is fair to say that we used a very robust analysis and found signatures of selection in biologically relevant regions.”

Reference: “Evidence of Selective Response in the Free-Breeding Dog Population in Chornobyl” by Megan N. Dillon, Reade B. Roberts, Jennifer A. Betz, Timothy A. Mousseau, Norman J. Kleiman and Matthew Breen, 26 September 2026, Genes. DOI: 10.3390/genes17101195
