Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

#6379. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

This story was updated on October 29, 2026 to include expert input from Emma Stone.

#6377. Divers Spent 7 Years Hunting a Ghost Ship Linked to a Nazi Spy Plot. They Just Found It.

A citizen-led search found the SS Cornwallis—and revived a forgotten Nazi spy story in Maine.

For seven years, a group of volunteer divers scoured historical records and the coast of Maine in search of one of New England’s largest undiscovered World War II shipwrecks. Now the SS Cornwallis has been found. The Nomad Exploration Team located the Canadian merchant vessel, which a German U-boat sank off Mount Desert Rock in 1944. The discovery also helps tell the story of the 43 people aboard the boat who lost their lives in the attack and revives interest in the German spies linked to the sinking.

The team used side-scan sonar to map the ocean floor where they believed the Cornwallis might rest, and they nearly overlooked the 400-foot, 5,458-ton vessel. Some of the group’s most harrowing dives later confirmed that the sonar anomaly really was the lost ship. “It was exhilaration,” said Danny Allan, a founding team member, according to Seacoastonline.

The nine-member, New Hampshire-based team began the search in 2019 with a rough location about 10 miles southwest of Mount Desert Rock. By drawing on historical records, the ship’s blueprints, and local fishermen’s observations, they narrowed the search to three likely sites. Even so, the work wasn’t going to be easy.

“There are big tides up off the Mount Desert area,” team member Jeff Goodreau told the Portland Press Herald. “A lot of weather, a lot of fog … Any way you look at it, the challenge is just getting there, whether it’s a five-hour run from Portsmouth or trailering a boat up there.”

In fact, the team nearly missed the wreck twice. On a first pass within 300 feet of it, they didn’t recognize the sonar image. Later, while they were reprogramming the GPS, they almost skipped past it again when it showed up just 100 feet away. “We would’ve written off that whole section as ‘we already looked there’ and wouldn’t have found it,” Allan said.

Reaching the wreck, nearly 400 feet down, was just as tricky. Team member Don Ferrara called it the scariest dive he’d ever done, and Goodreau described the site as deep, cold, and full of current. Still, “We were over the moon,” Ferrara said of the find.

“You’re the first person to see and touch this wreck literally in 80 years, so you’re ecstatic,” Allan said. “But it’s also extremely sobering because this is a grave. 43 souls lost their lives on this wreck.”

The tragedy happened in the Gulf of Maine as the Canadian ship was heading home to Saint John, New Brunswick, after loading sugar and molasses in Barbados. At 6 a.m. on December 3, 1944, the German submarine U-1230 fired a single torpedo that struck the forward cargo hold, and the Cornwallis sank in less than 10 minutes, according to the team. Only five of the 48 people aboard, most of them Canadian, survived. Fishing boats picked up the survivors, and a U.S. Navy vessel then carried them to Rockland, Maine.

The Cornwallis wasn’t a target the U-boat had been hunting. “The U-boat wasn’t looking for them,” Ferrara said. “They were just there.”

The sinking alerted the U.S. to the U-boat’s presence and prompted an investigation into its mission. By interviewing witnesses in Hancock, the FBI learned about Germany’s Operation Elster (Operation Magpie in English). Just days before the attack, the same submarine had landed two German spies, Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh, near Hancock Point. Their mission was to gather intelligence in the United States. The pair took a taxi to Bangor, a train to Portland, and then made their way to New York City. In the end, the plot fell apart from within: Colepaugh lost his nerve, confided in a friend, and turned himself in, which led to both men’s capture.

This wasn’t the first time the Cornwallis had been torpedoed. The ship was built in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1921. In 1942, a torpedo struck it while it was anchored at Barbados, and it partially sank in shallow water. After repairs, it returned to service.

“For the team, finding the wreck was the culmination of years of persistence,” Allan said in a statement, according to MassLive. “For the families and communities connected to the ship, it brings renewed attention to a largely forgotten tragedy.”

The Cornwallis is the latest find for the team, which had already located the USS Eagle 56 and the SS William H. Machen. “I love history,” Allan said. “My father was a history teacher. Other people like to see pretty fish and reefs. For me, I love to go see wrecks.”

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6373. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6367. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

Craftsman is getting in on the Advent-calendar game this holiday season. The iconic red-and-black tool brand’s first limited edition box set is back in stock and bound to sell out fast. All in all, it amounts to $200 worth of stuff—including a battery voucher—reasonably priced at just $65.

That includes an 8-inch ratchet, a magnetic bit driver with 11 bits, two sets of sockets, and two stubby screwdrivers.

There’s also a magnetic pickup tool that was strong enough to lift a multitool and a folded pocket knife off my desk. Most of the loot fits inside the hard case hiding behind Door Number One. Like a kid putting a puzzle together, I had fun fitting each item inside and snapping the case shut.

As you can probably guess, this Advent calendar isn’t all serious business. There’s no chocolate or booze inside, but there is a deck of playing cards, a cute key-chain tape measure, and—my favorite—a bottle opener with a retro acetate handle.

Just keep in mind that this Advent calendar isn’t meant to replace a compact tool kit—something we think makes a great stocking stuffer for the person in your life who loves to tinker.

#6364. NASA’s Swift telescope faced a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s tenure has ended, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. On November 4, Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere, where it was expected to burn up. This fiery end capped an uncontrollable fall from space.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift was doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6363. Tiny Arctic bacterium has an unexpected strategy for capturing carbon dioxide

Scientists discover an Arctic bacterium with an unusual metabolism that combines acetone consumption, sunlight, and carbon dioxide fixation.

A tiny bacterium drifting through the surface waters of the Arctic Ocean has been hiding an unusual metabolic trick.

It can’t eat sugar and it carries one of the smallest genomes of any marine microbe. And yet it thrives by doing something no one had documented in the marine world before.

This unusual organism appears equipped to break down acetone while incorporating dissolved carbon dioxide into its metabolism.

Researchers at Concordia University in Montreal and Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh have described the organism, Porticoccus arcticus, in a recent study.

Acetone is one of the most common volatile organic compounds floating around in seawater. It’s produced by phytoplankton, broken down from organic matter, and deposited from the atmosphere.

Arctic surface waters contain concentrations above 40 nanomolar – enough, it turns out, to sustain microbes.

The researchers first confirmed the concept in a related species, Porticoccus hydrocarbonoclasticus, a bacterium previously isolated from a lab culture.

When they offered it acetone as its only food, it grew. Its cell density was directly tied to how much acetone was available.

Higher concentrations actually proved toxic, which makes a certain biological sense. This is an organism tuned for scarcity, not abundance.

P. arcticus caught the team’s attention through metagenome-assembled genomes pulled from Canada Basin water samples.

Its genome is strikingly compact – just 1.29 million base pairs with a GC content of 41.6%.

For context, its closest well-characterized relative, P. hydrocarbonoclasticus, carries a genome nearly twice that size at 2.47 million base pairs and 53.1% GC content.

Its streamlined genome suggests that evolution has favored a compact set of genes suited to life in nutrient-poor waters.

It has no sugar transporters. Its glycolytic pathway is incomplete. It can’t break down glucose the way most bacteria do.

What it has kept, though, is telling. A complete acetone carboxylation pathway sits right there in the genome.

The other surprise is the light-harvesting equipment. P. arcticus carries two proteorhodopsin genes – molecular light-driven proton pumps – and neither one appears to be ancestral.

Phylogenetic analysis shows they were picked up through lateral gene transfer from distantly related bacteria, one from a Gammaproteobacterium and the other from a Betaproteobacterium.

The blue-light-absorbing proteorhodopsin dominates expression by a factor of roughly 64 over the green-light version.

That’s a sensible adaptation for an organism living in Arctic surface waters, where blue light penetrates farthest.

A carotenoid biosynthesis pathway also appears nearby, suggesting that the bacterium has additional machinery involved in producing pigments and protecting its cells from light-related damage.

“This organism has evolved a fascinating metabolic strategy,” said corresponding author David Walsh, a professor of biology at Concordia University.

“It combines the use of acetone as a carbon source with light-driven energy production, allowing it to thrive in nutrient-poor Arctic waters where other bacteria struggle to survive.”

This isn’t some boutique organism lurking at the edges of Arctic microbial communities.

The team analyzed microbial samples collected between 2017 and 2023 across a broad stretch of the Arctic Ocean.

P. arcticus showed up consistently. At some surface sites in the Canada Basin, it represented up to 9% of all 16S rRNA gene sequences at 5 and 20 meters depth.

It had a clear habitat preference: oligotrophic surface waters with intermediate sea ice cover. It was abundant at open ocean sites experiencing dynamic, year-to-year changes in ice conditions.

At permanently ice-covered stations and in deeper water layers, its numbers dropped sharply.

The real biogeochemical kicker is the carbon dioxide angle. P. arcticus carries a cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase.

This is an enzyme that converts dissolved CO2 into bicarbonate, the form its acetone carboxylase needs as a substrate.

So the acetone carboxylation isn’t just about eating acetone.

The acetone carboxylation reaction incorporates one molecule of inorganic carbon for every acetone molecule processed, linking acetone metabolism directly to carbon fixation.

“It’s a form of photoheterotrophy we haven’t seen before in the ocean,” Walsh said.

“This bacterium uses sunlight for energy while consuming acetone and fixing CO2 – it’s operating at the intersection of several metabolic strategies that were previously thought to be separate.”

The Arctic Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean basin on Earth.

As Arctic sea ice retreats and ocean conditions change, the habitat available to P. arcticus could shift, potentially altering its role in regional carbon cycling.

An organism that simultaneously consumes a volatile organic compound and fixes CO2 while being powered by light could play a larger role in Arctic carbon cycling than previously assumed.

The team is careful to note that the acetone carboxylation pathway they’ve identified could exist in other marine photoheterotrophs as well.

Its abundance in Arctic surface waters suggests that this previously overlooked metabolic pathway could have broader ecological importance.

Acetone degradation via carboxylation had only been described in terrestrial bacteria before this work.

The discovery reveals an overlooked pathway in the Arctic carbon cycle, suggesting that even the smallest ocean microbes may influence how carbon moves through the environment.

The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

#6360. Exercise may be one of the most overlooked treatments for depression

Psychiatrists say doctors should prescribe exercise more clearly because physical activity may improve depression, memory, and mental health.

A five-minute walk can sound easy until depression has taken away your energy. Then a doctor’s advice to get more exercise may leave you wondering where to begin.

Trials show that exercise can ease symptoms of depression.

Three Canadian psychiatrists argue that doctors should prescribe exercise with the same care and attention they give antidepressant medications.

Carl Zhou and Nicholas Fabiano work in the psychiatry department at the University of Ottawa, and Stanley Wong works in the psychiatry department at the University of Toronto.

Their opinion piece draws on earlier research, with no new experiment of their own.

“We still tend to treat exercise as general lifestyle advice,” Zhou said.

“The evidence we reviewed supports something more deliberate: a prescription that names the type of activity, the frequency, the intensity, the duration, the safety considerations, and a plan for follow-up, just as we would for a medication.”

A muscle doesn’t just move a limb when it contracts. It also releases molecules called myokines, which may interact with chemical pathways involved in mood and thinking.

Researchers call that proposed connection the muscle-brain axis. The authors discuss it as one explanation for what exercise does, while making room for several others.

The brain needs a healthy blood supply and metabolism, and it needs inflammation kept under control. Learning, meanwhile, means changing the connections between its cells.

Exercise influences the heart, blood vessels, immune system, and growth signals that help with learning.

Better sleep, more confidence and social contact, and lower risks of blood vessel and metabolic disease may help explain its effects as well.

Kirk Erickson’s team spent a year studying exercise and the brains of 120 older adults without dementia.

In that 2011 trial, half the volunteers did moderate aerobic exercise, while the rest did stretching.

The team was interested in the hippocampus, which helps us remember things.

This region grew by about two percent in the aerobic group, mainly at the front, but shrank in the stretching group.

The researchers described the increase as reversing one to two years of age-related shrinkage.

Among those who exercised, greater growth went along with greater improvement on a memory test.

Being active has also been linked to better thinking skills and lower risks of dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

Those links come largely from watching people’s habits, so those studies alone can’t tell us that exercise made the difference.

Researchers have put exercise to the test for depression and anxiety in randomized trials, letting chance decide who goes into each group.

The results show that activity programs can ease symptoms.

Walking and jogging helped, as did yoga and strength training.

A 2024 review in The BMJ reached that finding after bringing together 218 trials with 14,170 people who had depression.

More intense exercise generally brought greater relief, but there were reasons to be cautious about the research.

Only one trial passed the reviewers’ strictest check for avoiding bias, and their confidence in the findings was low or very low.

Someone struggling to exercise may find the next finding more encouraging.

A 2022 analysis of 15 long-term studies, covering 191,130 adults, found a link with lower depression risk even below the recommended activity level.

People who did about half the recommended amount had an 18% lower risk than those who reported no activity. Those doing the full amount had a 25% lower risk.

These studies observed people’s habits, so the figures don’t prove cause and effect. The largest difference appeared between doing nothing and doing a little.

For patients who can’t reach the full target, the authors suggest about 75 minutes of moderate activity a week as a place to start.

That’s roughly half the usual recommended minimum.

Medicines for schizophrenia offer limited help with thinking difficulties, even though those difficulties affect how a person manages everyday life. Exercise may have something to offer there.

Ten trials involving 385 people with schizophrenia went into a 2017 analysis, which found better overall thinking with aerobic exercise.

Exercise also showed potential benefits for working memory, which helps people hold and use information, and social cognition, which helps them understand others.

People with schizophrenia and other severe mental illnesses tend to spend long hours sitting and have high rates of heart disease, metabolic disease, and early death.

The authors point partly to the illness, social disadvantage, and the metabolic side effects of some medicines.

“In schizophrenia, exercise can work on psychiatric symptoms, cognition, and physical health at the same time, in a population with substantial unmet needs in all three,” Wong said.

The thinking results came from only a few small trials, though.

The World Health Organization recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults, plus muscle-strengthening work on at least two days.

Brisk walking counts as moderate; for vigorous activity, such as running or fast cycling, the range is 75 to 150 minutes.

A patient doesn’t have to begin at that level.

If depression has drained their energy, motivation, and concentration, the first step might be a five-minute walk, a walk with the dog, or exercises in a chair.

“The starting point does not have to be impressive,” Fabiano said. “It has to be possible.”

For most patients, the authors suggest a low-risk activity that they can gradually do more of.

Pain or dizziness may signal a need to adjust the exercise plan, while chest pain or severe breathlessness calls for immediate medical attention.

Others may need a medical check, physiotherapy, supervision, or a brief pause before increasing their activity.

That includes people who are frail or have unstable heart or breathing symptoms, recent falls or fainting, an infection, or uncontrolled pain.

Wong wants larger trials to find out whether the thinking gains seen in schizophrenia hold up. The existing trials leave that question open.

Researchers are also exploring exercise mimetics, drugs or other agents that might copy some of the chemical changes exercise causes.

These could, in theory, help with depression in people whose symptoms, disability, or frailty prevent them from moving enough.

The authors see these as a possible addition to treatment, with safe activity continuing wherever it is possible.

They also point out that exercise prescriptions could widen health gaps if patients can’t get the help they need to follow them.

They want funded community exercise programs, help with transportation, and partnerships with recreation and community centers.

The goal is not to turn every patient into an athlete, but to make physical activity a realistic, supported part of mental health treatment.

The opinion piece is published in the journal Brain Health.
