#6358. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:

#6357. Webb discovers something unexpected in the ice of an interstellar comet

Webb reveals unusual ice in interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS that closely resembles icy objects beyond Neptune, offering clues to planet formation.

Ice from a comet born around another star looks surprisingly different from the ice in most comets in our solar system.

But far beyond Neptune, scientists have found icy bodies that share its unusual characteristics.

If that match holds, the icy material that builds planets may take a similar form around more than one star.

The comet is 3I/ATLAS, only the third object from outside our solar system that astronomers have ever identified.

New measurements from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope show that its ice grains are tiny and mixed with dust.

Silvia Protopapa of the Southwest Research Institute led the study.

“Interstellar comets are small icy bodies that formed in the disks of gas and dust around other stars and are now passing through our solar system,” she said.

“As 3I/ATLAS warms up, gas escaping from its interior carries ice and dust grains into the surrounding cloud, or coma. Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born.”

The observations came from a Webb program set up to study interstellar visitors.

Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America leads that program and co-wrote the paper.

“We designed this program to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time,” Cordiner said.

His team wanted to learn what the comet’s ice, dust, and gas could reveal about how planetesimals, the building blocks of planets, form around other stars.

The team observed 3I/ATLAS three times with Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph, before and after the comet’s closest pass by the Sun.

The visits came on August 6, 2025, December 22, 2025, and April 1, 2026.

The instrument uses a prism to split light into its wavelengths, which shows what a material is made of and its physical state.

On the first visit, the comet was about 307 million miles (494 million kilometers) from the Sun. By the last one, it was about 530 million miles (853 million kilometers) away and heading back out.

Webb also detected water vapor, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide gas around the comet.

Water ice absorbs infrared light at specific wavelengths, creating dips in the light that astronomers measure.

Astronomers call the dips absorption bands. Infrared wavelengths are measured in microns, and one micron is about 1/25,000 of an inch.

Ice makes a deep dip near 3 microns and two weaker ones near 1.5 and 2.0 microns. Most icy comets show all three. In 3I/ATLAS, the 3-micron band was strong, but the 1.5- and 2.0-micron bands were very weak or missing.

“That combination was a puzzle,” Protopapa said. “The strong 3-micron band points to water ice in the coma. But the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets.”

To find out what kind of grain could produce that pattern, the team compared the measurements with detailed models of how light scatters off grains of different sizes and makeups.

The best fits came from grains about a micron across or smaller, made of water ice mixed with dust.

In grains that small and that dusty, light travels only a short distance through the ice. That weakens the 1.5- and 2.0-micron bands but leaves the 3-micron band strong.

Scientists think the ice grains in other comets are fairly pure, perhaps with a small amount of dust.

“The grains of 3I/ATLAS are about the same size as those in our own comets,” Protopapa said. “What seems to set them apart is how much dust is mixed into the ice.”

The grains around the comet didn’t stay the same from one visit to the next. By April 2026, as 3I/ATLAS moved away from the Sun, the data favored an extra set of ice-rich grains.

These were larger than the grains seen earlier, but still around a micron in size.

In April, Webb’s measurements also showed a faint feature that fits crystalline ice, meaning ice whose molecules are lined up in a regular pattern.

The ice may have been crystalline at the first and last visits, with the change coming mostly from grain size and the amount of dust. Or it may have started out in a more disordered form and become crystalline later.

Michael Kelley of the University of Maryland is the paper’s second author.

“We can’t yet tell whether the changes over time are the result of the Sun heating the grains differently at each observation, or of new material exposed as the comet’s surface eroded near the Sun,” Kelley said.

“Both are possible, and telling them apart is one of the open questions we aim to address.”

The team then compared 3I/ATLAS with Webb measurements of trans-Neptunian objects. These are icy bodies that orbit the Sun beyond Neptune, and scientists think they still hold material from the early solar system.

In 3I/ATLAS, the 3-micron band has a shape much like the one seen in several groups of these objects.

The resemblance is strongest for groups whose light also shows clear signs of carbon dioxide ice and organic compounds.

The likeness is in the water-ice band, not in the carbon dioxide. And like the comet, these objects lack strong 1.5- and 2.0-micron bands.

“At first glance, 3I/ATLAS looks different from the icy comets we know,” Protopapa said. “But when we placed it alongside distant icy worlds in our own solar system, it no longer looked out of place.”

If later observations confirm the pattern, the physical form of water ice may be established early in the disks where planets form. Icy bodies born in those disks may then preserve some of those original characteristics.

The team had just one interstellar comet to work with, and astronomers had identified only two objects from beyond the solar system before it.

Nobody can yet say whether ice this dusty is common among visitors from other stars.

Future Webb observations could reveal whether 3I/ATLAS is an unusual visitor or evidence that icy worlds form in surprisingly similar ways across the galaxy.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

#6355. Ancient viruses left behind genes that are still spreading millions of years later

Ancient virus genes moved between yeast species, possibly with help from insects, revealing a surprising way evolution works.

Genes usually move down a family tree, from parents to their offspring.

In a group of yeasts that live on rotting wood, a bundle of genes left behind by an ancient virus has also moved sideways, from one species into another.

A new genetic study found evidence of at least three of those crossings.

As far as the researchers know, it’s the first documented case of a whole cluster of genes from an ancient RNA virus moving between species.

Derek Taylor, a biologist at the University at Buffalo, did the work with master’s student Dominic Tringali.

They suspect that wood-eating insects, which carry these yeasts in their guts and leave them in their droppings, brought different species close enough to swap DNA.

“It’s an evolutionary whodunit, and wood-eating insects had the means and opportunity,” said Taylor, a professor in the university’s Department of Biological Sciences.

All of the evidence came from DNA. The team compared publicly available genomes from 18 yeast species and strains rather than watching a transfer happen in the lab.

The genes came from a totivirus, a kind of virus that infects fungi, including yeasts. It mostly passes from one generation of cells to the next when a cell divides.

Totiviruses carry their genes as RNA and have no built-in way to write themselves into a host’s DNA, the way HIV does.

Even so, a copy of one ended up in an ancestor of these yeasts, which belong to a group called Scheffersomyces.

Exactly how that happened isn’t known. The researchers propose that the yeast cell itself copied the viral RNA into DNA.

Taylor and a colleague first described the cluster in a 2009 paper, working with a yeast called Scheffersomyces stipitis. The cluster holds four genes in a row.

One of them carries both of the virus’s main parts, the instructions for its protein shell and for the enzyme that copies its RNA.

The other three are extra copies of the shell gene alone, made after the virus’s genes joined the yeast’s DNA.

The team named the cluster STORM. In the yeasts where it was first found, it has held the same spot in the genome for at least 15 million years. It may be much older.

If genes pass only from parent to offspring, their family tree should match the family tree of the species that carry them. STORM’s tree didn’t.

In two of the crossings, the cluster in one group of yeasts looked most like the cluster in a more distant group. Biologists call this kind of sideways move horizontal gene transfer.

It’s well known among microbes, and it has been documented in fungi and even plants.

To see how unusual STORM’s pattern was, the team built family trees for 3,527 other genes shared by all 18 yeasts. None of those trees reproduced any of the three STORM patterns in full.

“Now we have compelling evidence that an entire four-gene cluster has crossed species boundaries,” Taylor said.

Crossbreeding between species could in principle produce a similar pattern.

But it would have taken at least two separate episodes, and the team found no sign that the donor species’ DNA had spread widely through the rest of the genome.

The third crossing replaced only part of the cluster. In one strain of S. stipitis, the first three genes were swapped for versions that most resemble those of a related species, Scheffersomyces segobiensis.

The fourth gene and the DNA on either side kept their S. stipitis ancestry.

One crossing left more evidence behind than the others.

Beside STORM in a yeast called Scheffersomyces insectosa, the team found the broken remains of a jumping gene.

These stretches of DNA, known as transposons, can move from one place in a genome to another.

The researchers named this family of transposons YEET, short for Yeast Endogenous Element Transposon.

Its remains near STORM, and a broken yeast gene next to them, both looked like they came from the same donor group as STORM itself.

“Because STORM and a neighboring jumping gene show evidence of the same unusual evolutionary history, we suspect the transposon may have carried STORM between yeast species as extra cargo,” Tringali said.

YEET transposons appear to have crossed between these rotting-wood yeasts on their own, too, in at least five cases. How the other full-cluster crossing happened remains unclear.

Scheffersomyces yeasts share living space in rotting logs, in insect droppings, and inside the guts of wood-eating insects.

One species in the group, described as new in 2025, was isolated from the cocoon wall of a stag beetle.

“In order to exchange genomic material, you have to be in the same place at the same time,” Taylor said.

The authors wrote that these shared homes give different yeasts chances to swap DNA. Contact alone, though, doesn’t show how the DNA actually moved.

RNA viruses change quickly, and genes borrowed from them are generally expected to slow down once they become part of a host’s genome. STORM went the other way.

The team estimated that its proteins changed about seven times faster than those of related viruses that still infect cells.

Depending on how old the researchers assumed the cluster to be, the estimate ranged from just under six to nearly nine times faster.

“These genes have had an extraordinary evolutionary afterlife,” Tringali said. “Long after the original virus disappeared, its genes continued to evolve, multiply and spread between yeast species.”

The four genes didn’t all change in the same way. The fourth gene changed the most.

Tests suggested that natural selection weakened on that gene and let changes build up, rather than favoring new versions of it.

Yet that gene held on to a key part of one of the virus’s tricks. Related yeast viruses take the protective chemical cap off the front of the cell’s own RNA messages and use it on their own.

The fourth gene still carries the amino acids that form the virus’s cap-holding pocket.

Selection on the first gene grew stronger instead, compared with the second and third.

Computer predictions of protein shapes suggested that all four genes still carry instructions for proteins shaped like a virus shell.

The cluster isn’t silent. In genetic data from five yeast species and strains, cells were making RNA copies of all four genes, and the first gene was usually the most active.

In one species, the first and fourth genes were about three times as active in flasks built to mix in more oxygen.

Those growth tests weren’t designed to probe viral infection, so the genes’ activity could be tied to RNA handling, to the yeasts’ surroundings, or to defense against viruses.

There’s a hint for that last idea. In a 2018 experiment, a shell-like gene from another yeast, Debaryomyces hansenii, cleared a related virus out of baker’s yeast.

Of the two S. segobiensis strains, the one with an intact cluster carried no detectable totivirus. The one without an intact cluster was the only strain in the survey that did.

“Totiviruses are kind of like a frenemy for yeast. Under some conditions, they help the host deal with physiological stress,” Taylor said.

“So it might be useful for a yeast to keep a virus’ benefits around without having to worry about controlling the virus.”

What the four STORM proteins actually do inside a yeast cell is still untested.

The team hopes to grow the yeasts under different kinds of stress and see whether the genes respond.

The results could point to the job the genes now do for their hosts.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Biology and Evolution.

#6354. The 8 Best Electric Scooters Built for the Daily Commute—And Beyond

These reliable models give you a comfortable, safe commute and offer good range, top speeds, and anti-theft features.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Instead of driving for every short trip to the store or commute to work, hop on an electric scooter and zoom through your neighborhood. Electric scooters are easier to ride than electric skateboards and more portable than electric bikes, so they’re a great alternative for city-dwellers who don’t have the space for a car or would prefer a smaller mode of transportation for short distances.

These days, there are plenty of affordable and durable electric scooters available. Options range from electric scooters built for just a few miles of daily commuting to ones designed to handle uneven trails, high speeds, and long distances. We tried out electric scooters on our own commutes to find the best.

What Are the Laws for Riding E-Scooters?In many areas, electric scooters aren’t allowed on sidewalks, so check whether you need to ride in bike lanes before you jet around. Some areas have speed limits on small electric vehicles like scooters and e-bikes. For instance, in Florida, e-scooters with seats must be registered and have a title and license plate, so check your local laws before you opt for one of our seated options. Similarly, there are some restrictions based on battery size and type.

If you’re looking for a scooter that can do just about everything well—with a long range to boot—check out the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max. It can go up to 40 miles on a single charge, handle slopes up to 22 degrees, and carry riders up to 265 pounds.

Its 10-inch pneumatic tires are great at absorbing bumps in the road, and it folds easily for storage. The tires are “self-sealing,” meaning an interior liner will automatically fill in punctures for a short-term patch. It’s not a permanent solution, but even if you roll over a nail or sharp rock, you’ll be able to continue driving without stopping for an immediate replacement. At just over 40 pounds, this Ninebot is heavier than some commuter scooters. But some of that comes from the bigger battery for extended range.

While 40 miles won’t take you on long-range adventures, it should last for multiple weeks of scootering around town. The Ninebot is the second most expensive of the scooters we recommend. But considering how well-rounded this e-scooter is, it’s the best for most people.

The GoTrax XR Elite needs to be on your radar if you’re looking for an electric scooter that doesn’t take a bite out of your wallet. At just 32 pounds, it’s one of the lightest and easiest to carry among the scooters here. This is further amplified by the foldable design and slender frame.

This scooter has an estimated range of 16 miles, a top speed of about 15 miles per hour, and a max incline of 15 degrees. What really sets it apart from the others is the affordable price given the quality performance. This costs about $400 less than the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max.

While the XR Elite isn’t built for long distances or top speeds, it’s a perfect choice for puttering around town. Moreover, its battery charges in just four hours, allowing you to get around sooner if need be.

Very few electric scooters offer the balance of affordability and performance that the Gotrax G3 Max does. With a maximum range of 37 miles, the scooter is ideal for daily commuting back and forth to work without the constant need to recharge.

Beyond this, the scooter is equipped with a number of features that caught our eye, including the integrated number lock on the body that dissuades thieves by preventing them from actually being able to unfold and ride the scooter without the right code.

The G3 Max also comes with an LED display showing your speed, speed modes, mileage, and battery life. There’s an LED headlight for riding at night too.

Full Gotrax G3 Max Electric Scooter Review

Don’t confuse this electric scooter with a bike or moped. Built with a seat and basket, the Flex Ultra from Gotrax is more than just a quick commuter.

When testing this scooter, I took it from Central Park all the way back to my apartment in Brooklyn. I had my backpack, which weighed over 20 pounds, in the basket, and I sat on the seat for the majority of the trip.

What I noticed immediately was the zip of the motor as I got close to 20 miles per hour on straightaways and churned up the incline of the Queensboro Bridge without losing momentum. I also have to admit that I loved the seat. Instead of standing for over 30 minutes on the ride back, I could rest a bit more while still making better time than I would on the subway.

The throttle is responsive, and the larger 14-inch wheels stood up well to the potholes on the streets and cracks on the pavement. While its size prevents it from being an easy storage item in a closet—even though it folds—this electric scooter comes with the power, comfort, and convenience for quick grocery trips and long city commutes alike.

With a 34-mile range and a top speed of 20 miles per hour, the Ninebot E3 Pro is an ideal commuter scooter balancing speed and range. It’s also quite durable, with an alloy frame boasting an IPX5 water resistance for riding through puddles, rain, and even mud.

Furthermore, the electric scooter is a relatively quick charge, going from zero to fully charged in 7 hours. This means you can plug it in overnight and ride out in the morning on a full charge with no worry. Alongside an LED headlight, the scooter comes with lighting underneath the board so you’ll have full visibility at night.

The headlight and under-board lighting are paired with real turn signals as well, so you don’t have to take your hands of the handles to let drivers around you know which direction you’re headed.

Full Segway E3 Pro Electric Scooter Review

This lightweight and affordable scooter won’t take you everywhere with just a 16 mile range, but you can take it anywhere you please. The scooter is small enough to fold up and carry without feeling like it’s dragging on your arm after a few minutes.

While it won’t exactly disappear under a desk, it’s probably one of the few that will fit with ease in a storage closet or under the bed at home. At the same time, you can toss it in the back of your trunk and take it out whenever you go to the park.

The hollow tires also mean you’ll never run flat and don’t need to worry about inflating them after a few winter months out of use.

Have you ever wanted to take a load off while riding but don’t want a permanent seat? The Gotrax Eclipse offers the best of both worlds. The electric scooter comes with a detachable seat so you can plop down if you know you have a long ride ahead, but can take it off and leave it at home when portability and foldability take priority.

The scooter is more than just the seat as well. With a top speed of 25 miles per hour and a max range of 38 miles, this is a performance-focused option that is great for longer commutes and open streets.

At the same time, the electric scooter has a small rear shelf that can be used to securely tie down small packages and backpacks so you can actually use it for carrying more than just yourself.

Reaching speeds of over 30 miles per hour and boasting a range of 45, this electric scooter from Segway is aptly named the SuperScooter GT3. This heavy-duty option is designed with performance as the end all, be all priority. In fact, in combination with its 11-inch self-sealing tires, the SuperScooter GT3 is one of the few electric scooters that is legitimately well-equipped to handle gravel, dirt, and general off-road adventures.

Beyond pure power and battery, the electric scooter comes with one of the most useful displays that we’ve found. The full color screen comes with smart technology that connects to your phone so you can receive notifications and access navigation routes in real time.

That said, before you click buy, make sure it’s actually legal to ride in your city. Electric scooters of this speed and size are often highly regulated and illegal to ride in densely populated cities across the United States.

An electric scooter’s range is based on battery and motor size and is impacted by a number of factors, including rider weight, weather conditions, surface type, and incline of the roads you travel on. The ranges we include are based on the manufacturers’ claims, and your real-world use will vary.

Many scooters get up to 10 miles, while some can last for up to 40 miles or more on a single charge. Some have various drive settings that help you get the most juice out of your battery based on the type of ride you’re on. For instance, if you’re trying to conserve power for a longer trip, many options have a low-power or eco mode, which reduces top speed or acceleration for the sake of saving the battery. Furthermore, if you want to extend your scooter range as much as possible, consider routing yourself on smooth flat roads with little incline that don't require lots of stopping and starting.

Most of the e-scooters we recommend top out between 15 and 20 mph. That should be fast enough to zip along city streets and paths without feeling like you’re falling behind.

The only exception to this speed range is the Navee XT5 electric scooter, which reaches a top speed of 31 mph. However, if you’re seeking a quicker commute or more of a thrill, there are other e-scooters that reach speeds up to 60 mph. We didn’t recommend any of those because many states and cities have banned them or require you to gain an additional license to use them.

Electric scooters often have motors with a power rating between 250 and 350 watts. This is enough for most daily city commuting. If you’re a heavier person or expected to ride up steep inclines, you may want to opt for a scooter with a larger, more powerful motor. High wattage motors offer significantly more torque and acceleration but typically come at a premium. Their size also makes them heavier than lower wattage motors, which can make the scooter more cumbersome to carry or transport when not in use.

Almost all electric scooters have rubber tires, whether they’re solid, tubeless, or tires with inner tubes. Solid rubber tires are the longest-lasting and are ideal for those making shorter rides on smooth streets, but they also absorb less shock than their tubeless counterparts.

Tires with inner tubes were more common in the past, but we’re starting to see more tubeless and tube-ready tires today. Both tubeless and tube-ready tires can suffer punctures, but offer more cushioning during a ride than solid rubber models.

If you plan on riding a scooter in the early morning or night, look for a scooter with good front and rear lights. It’s also a good idea to look for a scooter with a horn or bell to warn bikers, pedestrians, and other scooter riders that you’re approaching. Some high end scooters also come with board lights and turn signals for additional visibility in the dark.

All scooters should have good brakes as well. Some only have them on one wheel, but more powerful scooters that need to decelerate quickly should have front and back brakes, and possibly a motor brake so you don’t go flying down a hill faster than intended. Motor brakes can also provide some regenerative braking, extending the scooter’s range slightly as you ride.

Some other extras to look for on electric scooters are items like seats or baskets. These are great to have if you prefer a seated ride and/or if you plan on using the scooter for errands, like grocery shopping.

In selecting these electric scooters, we rode multiple options. We used the scooters in daily work commutes to test their power, speed, range, and comfort over distance. This included trips over long bridges, on steep inclines, and many times, on streets without bike lanes. We also gauged how the acceleration and brakes felt in our hands, and how smooth the scooter stayed when riding over bumps or uneven asphalt.

For scooters we haven’t tested yet, we based our picks on research, evaluating the opinions and ratings of professional reviewers, as well as checking out customer reviews and rankings, and evaluating each model’s most important specs like wattage, range, and safety features. We chose reputable brands, selecting electric scooters that are not only the highest-performing models on the market, but also the easiest to find in stock.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. #6353. A generation feeling powerless: College students are overwhelmed by climate anxiety

New research reveals widespread climate anxiety among college students, with many feeling powerless and universities facing calls to provide more support.

Only four percent of college students in a recent survey reported feeling hopeful about the climate crisis frequently or “a lot.”

Many others reported a bleak mix of powerlessness, frustration, and anxiety.

Yet universities may not be doing enough to help students manage these difficult emotions.

That’s the uncomfortable takeaway from a pair of interdisciplinary studies out of the University of Utah.

Researchers surveyed hundreds of undergraduates about how climate change makes them feel and what, if anything, helps them cope.

The research team, led by environmental scientist Jennifer Follstad Shah and psychologist Monika Lohani, surveyed 547 students enrolled across three environmental studies courses and one communication course.

They asked a simple question: when you think about climate change, what do you feel?

Fifty-four percent of students reported feeling powerless frequently or “a lot.” Fifty-five percent said the same about frustration.

Anger, worry, fear, and anxiety clustered right behind, each hitting the “a lot” category for roughly one in five students. Meanwhile, 58 percent said they never felt happiness about the climate situation.

Only four percent reported feeling hopeful frequently or “a lot.” Even when students who experienced hope less often were included, the figure reached just 40 percent.

Here’s where the study gets interesting. Environmental studies majors did score higher on the researchers’ Climate Anxiety Index.

But once the statistical models accounted for other variables, a student’s major stopped being a significant predictor of climate anxiety altogether.

The final hierarchical regression model, which explained 52 percent of the variance in climate anxiety scores, pointed to different culprits.

These included political ideology, how often students encountered climate information, whether they ranked climate change as a top personal concern, and their levels of general anxiety.

“They’re not alone,” Shah said. “There’s a lot of students feeling that way, and likely a lot of adults feeling that way.”

The relationship between climate anxiety and generalized anxiety turned out to be striking.

Climate anxiety and general anxiety were closely related, although the researchers could not determine whether one contributed to the other.

Students with moderate-to-high climate anxiety tended to report low-to-moderate general anxiety.

These findings suggest that climate and general anxiety are closely related but remain distinct psychological experiences.

“It may be that climate anxiety is a contributor to general anxiety, as well as the converse,” Shah said.

Gender told a similar nuanced story. Women in the study reported significantly higher general anxiety than men, and initially appeared more climate-anxious too.

But once general anxiety was accounted for, gender dropped out as a predictor entirely.

The findings suggest that differences in general anxiety, rather than gender itself, may help explain the higher climate anxiety initially reported by women.

Not all information sources hit the same way. Classroom learning and online media – especially social media – were both significant predictors of higher climate anxiety.

However, information from friends, family, and co-workers barely registered.

Fewer than 30 percent of students reported getting climate information from family or colleagues with any regularity.

The findings suggest that climate change may come up less often in everyday conversations than in classrooms or online.

One interaction caught the researchers’ attention. For students outside environmental studies, more online climate exposure correlated significantly with higher anxiety.

For environmental studies majors, that link vanished.

Some of these students described engaging in “hopescrolling” – deliberately curating their feeds toward solutions-focused content rather than doom.

Lohani’s companion study dug into what students actually do with all this distress. Some found relief in nature, pets, self-care, or learning more about the science itself.

“The knowledge is empowering them to understand the intricacies. That makes them not feel hopeless,” Lohani said.

“All the progress in terms of technology that has come out to combat the carbon footprint actually made them feel more hopeful.”

But many students described shutting down entirely. One wrote: “Sometimes I just don’t feel like doing anything at all because it makes me so anxious.”

“Those who are overwhelmed, they might be catastrophizing or using avoidance or distraction, which ultimately is not good for their well-being, or efforts to address the climate change crisis,” Lohani noted.

“Those who are apathetic towards it, that is not bad for their well-being in the short run, but ultimately it is affecting them and their community.”

Both researchers argued that campuses need to stop treating climate anxiety as background noise.

Their recommendations are concrete: establish climate anxiety support groups within counseling centers, fund cross-departmental forums for open discussion, and train instructors to expect emotional responses to climate material.

The University of Utah’s own environmental studies program has already begun hosting Good Grief Circles, modeled on the Good Grief Network co-founded by Laura Schmidt, a 2014 Utah graduate.

These peer support sessions give students space to process ecological distress without judgment.

“Don’t be afraid to talk about it and let people know that you feel this way,” Shah said. “There’s power in those bonds.”

The study has its limits – the sample skewed female (66 percent), White (69 percent), and politically left-leaning (63 percent).

It was drawn from a single university in the arid Mountain West, where shrinking Great Salt Lake levels and megadrought make climate impacts impossible to ignore.

The researchers are calling for broader studies across more diverse campuses and majors.

Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that climate anxiety extends beyond students majoring in environmental subjects.

It is closely linked to general anxiety and affects students across academic disciplines, raising questions about whether universities provide enough emotional support.

The students surveyed said, overwhelmingly, that they want more opportunities to talk about it. The question is whether anyone’s listening.

The study is published in the journal Sustainability.

#6351. Restaurant cooking is becoming a surprisingly major source of air pollution

Restaurant cooking is emerging as a major source of urban air pollution, sometimes exceeding vehicle exhaust emissions during peak dining hours.

The smell of food drifting out of a restaurant rarely makes people think of air pollution.

Yet new research shows that in parts of central London and Beijing, cooking releases more fine particles than vehicle exhaust during lunch and dinner hours.

Cleaner vehicles and tighter exhaust rules appear to have helped change that balance. Kitchens have faced less attention: UK and European rules require them to extract fumes, but do not require filters.

Ben Langford, an atmospheric scientist at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, led the research.

His team measured emissions from one central neighborhood each in London, Beijing and Delhi, three cities with more than 10 million people.

“Most people smell cooking but never consider it as a pollutant, yet cooking can release large amounts of fine particulate matter into the atmosphere,” Langford said.

The team placed instruments on London’s BT Tower, 623 feet (190 meters) above the street, and on a Beijing tower at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics, 335 feet (102 meters) up.

In Old Delhi, they worked 108 feet (33 meters) above ground at Indira Gandhi Delhi Technical University for Women.

Above the rooftops, a wind sensor and an instrument that identifies chemicals in particles took readings five times a second.

Matching the air’s upward and downward movements with what it carried showed how much pollution came from the surrounding neighborhood.

Frying oil, car exhaust and coal fires produce different chemical mixtures, which helped the team trace particles to their sources.

To measure pollution moving through the air, the researchers separated their readings into upward and downward air movements.

These tiny particles can travel deep into the lungs, and some may enter the bloodstream.

In London, cooking produced up to 83% of the measured particle emissions at midday and 87% in the early evening. In Beijing, those shares reached 61% and 76%.

Both towers overlooked areas with many restaurants, and the researchers think commercial frying produced most of the cooking smoke.

At some hours, traffic contributed less than 10% of local emissions in both cities.

Beijing’s cooking emissions were about 75% higher in winter than summer, partly perhaps because the wind changed direction.

Winter winds mostly brought air from restaurants and commercial buildings to the northwest, while summer winds brought more air from a highway to the east.

Europe has tightened exhaust standards in stages since 1992.

London also introduced a congestion charge and an ultra-low emission zone, and its restrictions on polluting solid fuels helped keep coal and wood smoke barely detectable.

Study co-author Eiko Nemitz, also at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, pointed to the success of traffic controls.

“Air quality policies targeting vehicle exhaust emissions have been highly effective,” Nemitz said. “As a result, cooking emissions are now a surprisingly important and poorly regulated part of the urban pollution mix.”

Earlier research in New York found a similar shift, with cooking, wildfire smoke and chemical products becoming increasingly important sources of summertime particle pollution.

Old Delhi told a different story: cooking accounted for 8% of direct particle emissions over an average day, while traffic contributed 56%.

Yet its cooking emissions per unit of area exceeded central London’s in winter and were only about 35% lower in summer.

Cooking’s small share reflects the much larger contribution from traffic and other burning.

The Delhi site stood near busy roads, a railway station and a large bus terminal, and the area released roughly two to four times as much soot as central London.

Both Beijing and Delhi restrict diesel vehicles to nighttime hours. The researchers suggested that looser emission controls and more older vehicles help explain Delhi’s higher soot levels.

Kitchen exhaust filters may have less impact in Delhi, where many homes have poor ventilation and more cooking happens outdoors.

The authors said traffic and other burning should remain the main targets there.

The sources releasing particles locally did not match the mix already in the air.

Cooking accounted for just 5% to 10% of airborne fine particles in London and Beijing, while traffic contributed 5% to 18%.

Much of the pollution formed in the air from gases, including ammonia, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide. Many of these particles formed across the wider region, beyond the city center.

Particles formed this way accounted for 59% to 63% of the total in London’s and Beijing’s air, compared with 30% in Delhi.

Most of Delhi’s particles were organic material, from both local traffic and burning and distant sources such as farm fires.

The towers measured neighborhood emissions, but the air above them also contained pollution formed or carried in from elsewhere.

Cutting local emissions alone may therefore leave London and Beijing above World Health Organization guidelines, the authors wrote.

Most official pollution inventories leave cooking out. The UK counts cooking fuel but not smoke from the food, while European and global inventories omit cooking altogether.

The London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory added cooking recently.

Most of the BT Tower’s measurement area lies in Westminster, where the inventory put cooking at 44% of annual emissions after excluding brake and tire wear, close to the tower’s 45%.

Still, the inventory estimated about 76% more cooking emissions than the tower measured.

The winter measurements took place during the UK’s Plan B rules for the Omicron variant of COVID-19, introduced on December 8, 2021, which may have reduced restaurant and pub visits.

Cooking smoke also raises health concerns, as chefs face a higher risk of respiratory illness than other people.

Earlier research suggests fatty acids in cooking particles may help them stay airborne for days instead of hours.

Langford said better kitchen filtration could offer a relatively quick way to improve air quality.

“Over recent decades we have dramatically reduced emissions from road transport, but we have paid far less attention to emissions from commercial kitchens and food preparation,” Langford said.

“Our results suggest this is an area where further improvements in air quality could be achieved relatively quickly through better filtration of kitchen fumes.”

The study is published in the journal npj Climate and Atmospheric Science.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

#6349. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

#6348. Why are human brains so big? Hundreds of genetic switches may explain

Scientists identified hundreds of genetic switches that may help explain why human brains grow much larger than those of other great apes.

We share many of our genes with chimpanzees and gorillas, but our brains grow much larger. A new study suggests that part of the difference may come from how brain cells use those shared genes.

Researchers in Dresden grew brain tissue from stem cells belonging to all three species.

They found nearly 600 short stretches of DNA that were more accessible in human cells, many linked to genes that help cells take shape.

Mareike Albert led the work at the Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden, part of TUD Dresden University of Technology. Her group studies gene activity as the brain develops.

“Changes in brain size actually arise during development. This is when the majority of neurons are generated. But developing brain tissue of non-human great apes is not available for research, and for good ethical reasons,” said Albert.

To study those early stages, the team grew tiny balls of tissue called cerebral organoids.

With the right chemical signals, stem cells arrange themselves into tissue that copies some features of early brain development.

Study co-author Madeline Lancaster first grew cerebral organoids in 2013. She now runs a lab at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology.

The researchers used one gorilla stem cell line, one chimpanzee line and three human lines. They examined the organoids after eight weeks.

They also studied donated human fetal cortex, the brain’s outer region, from weeks 13 and 14 of pregnancy. This let them check how closely the organoids resembled developing human tissue.

The team focused on stem cells called basal radial glia. These cells divide deep within developing brain tissue and extend long arms toward its surface.

Researchers stained the outside of each organoid with a fluorescent dye, allowing them to identify cells whose long extensions reached the surface.

A cell sorter then separated the tissue into four groups.

These included the branching stem cells, related stem cells anchored near the fluid-filled center, cells that produce neurons, and neurons themselves.

The researchers checked which parts of the cells’ DNA were open and accessible to the machinery that reads it. Across the three species, they identified 225,395 stretches they could compare.

Of those, 599 were more accessible in human branching stem cells than in their chimpanzee and gorilla counterparts. All 599 were also accessible in the donated human tissue.

Theresa Schütze, who led the experimental work, explained how these stretches can affect genes.

“These genetic switches are short DNA sequences that control how active a gene is. You can think of them as sort of dimmers that turn genes up or down,” said Schütze.

“We found nearly 600 switches that are more active in human neural stem cells than in those of chimpanzees and gorillas,” Schütze said.

About 63% overlapped DNA regions already known to regulate gene activity. A few belonged to regions that changed unusually quickly after the human lineage split from other great apes.

A switch can control a gene some distance away along the DNA.

Using maps of how DNA folds inside cells, the researchers linked the 599 stretches to 589 possible target genes.

These genes help build the forebrain, attach cells to their neighbors, guide cells into position and grow nerve cell branches.

The team made its ape sequencing data available through the public Gene Expression Omnibus archive.

The researchers then examined whether these differences in DNA accessibility were reflected in gene activity.

They found 939 genes whose activity differed between human and chimpanzee branching stem cells, including 465 that were more active in humans.

Many of those more active genes help shape cells. To explore that pattern, the team gave each cell type a score based on the activity of its shape-related genes.

In chimpanzees, scores rose from the simpler, anchored stem cells to neurons. Human branching stem cells scored almost as highly as neurons.

That stood out because neurons develop elaborate shapes over months as they grow toward their targets. The human stem cells were using many of the same genes while they were still dividing.

The team then checked where else those 465 genes were active. In developing mouse brains, most worked in neurons.

In human and macaque fetal cortex, they worked in both neurons and stem cells. These were old, widely shared genes, rather than genes found only in humans.

The researchers think human branching stem cells have adopted part of the program that shapes neurons, a process called co-option.

This may help explain their more elaborate shapes and adds to earlier research focused on human-specific genes.

“It is not necessarily different genes that make a human brain special. As the nearly identical genomes suggest, we use largely the same toolkit as apes, just with different settings,” Albert said.

The team chose two of the 589 candidate genes for further tests. One, FAM107A, makes a protein that binds to actin, part of the internal scaffolding that supports a cell’s shape.

The other, CNGA3, helps form an ion channel best known for its role in the eye’s color-sensing cells. Chimpanzee organoids showed very little activity from this gene.

Its protein was plentiful in human radial glia, scarce in gorilla cells and undetectable in chimpanzee cells.

To test the switches themselves, researchers placed human and chimpanzee versions in mouse cells beside a reporter gene. A glow showed when a switch was working.

The human FAM107A switch produced a glow; the chimpanzee version did not. Both versions of the CNGA3 switch worked, but the human version worked more strongly.

The human CNGA3 switch carries a single DNA letter change that creates landing spots for 11 control proteins.

When researchers removed either gene from human organoids, fewer stem cells developed complex shapes.

Cells missing FAM107A also grew fewer branches from their cell bodies, and the organoids contained fewer young neurons.

Adding extra human FAM107A to chimpanzee organoids also made cells simpler. That suggests the amount matters: increasing this gene’s activity does not necessarily produce more branches.

Organoids capture only part of brain development.

They grow a thin version of the outer stem cell layer that develops during the second trimester, where much of the human cortex’s growth takes place.

The links between individual switches and genes also need more work.

When researchers reduced the activity of the FAM107A switch, rather than removing the gene, the gene’s activity barely changed.

Other switches may help keep it working. The result shows why changing one switch can have a different effect from removing an entire gene.

Testing two genes offers clues about how these cells develop, but it does not explain the contribution of all 589 candidates. Nor does the study measure how many extra neurons these differences might add to a human cortex.

The researchers suggest that better growth conditions, including a protein called LIF, might help organoids develop a fuller outer stem cell layer.

That would give scientists a better way to study a stage of development that matters greatly for brain size.

The findings suggest that the evolution of the human brain may depend not only on which genes we inherited, but also on how those genes are used during development.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.
