#6347. The 7 Best Camping Chairs You’ll Be Happy to Sink Your Butt Into

Roughing it doesn't mean you need a rough landing. We got our hands on models from Yeti, Coleman, REI Co-op, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A camping chair is the way to go if you want a comfortable place to sit around the campfire on your next camping trip. A quality camping chair balances portability with comfort, and some have features like thick, cushioned seats, footrests, or rocking bases. There are even camping chairs that pack down so small that you can fit them in your backpack—ideal for park concerts or to take backcountry camping.

Generally speaking, the most important things to look for are how easily the chair opens and collapses and how heavy or cumbersome it is to carry, along with the durability of the frame and seat material. Other considerations include weight capacity and the amount of support you get.

For this story, we stuck mainly to the classic collapsible camping chairs that work just as well for a week in the woods as they do sitting on your back patio. To help you narrow your search, our testers and I researched and then tested a selection of camping chairs, from the ultralight to the plush.

The newest camping chair from Yeti offers all the same quality of the Trailhead in a smaller, lighter, and more affordable package. The Trailhead Field is built with portability in mind, but doesn’t sacrifice comfort to do it.

The proprietary polyester blend Twilite fabric is flexible and smooth, while the aluminum frame sheds precious ounces without compromising too much durability. I actually enjoyed the Twilite fabric more than the the FlexGrid used in the original Trailhead. It has a bit more give and molded a bit better to my body, especially as I settled in.

It’s worth noting that the camping chair is much smaller than the original Trailhead, making it a lot easier to bring with you in the trunk of a small sedan without taking up too much space. That said, if you want a cup holder, you’ll have to pay an additional 20 bucks for the luxury.

Thanks to this affordable camping chair’s built-in insulated, four-can cooler, you can leave the kombuchas in the heavy cooler in the shade while you stash a few beer cans and a handful of ice in your chair.

Cooler sleeve aside, I also like this Coleman chair’s side pocket and cushioned backrest. The side pocket is big enough for books or tablets and has two mesh sections on the front for smaller items like bottle caps, keys, and a phone.

It has an above-average 325-pound weight limit. And while it isn’t the lightest camping chair on this list, I found its 8.5 pounds reasonable to transport, especially considering the attachments.

Make no mistake, this camping chair doesn’t lend itself well to extreme portability. But if you’re mostly car camping out of your truck or driving to a friend’s BBQ, you’ll love the extra size and support it offers.

Yeti’s Trailhead camping chair immediately stood out for its comfort. It’s made of a flexible, durable fabric that’s spread tight against the frame, with a weight limit of 500 pounds—the highest of any chair we tested. Despite its strength, the material wasn’t overly stiff either. There was enough give to cradle my legs and back, balancing out the support with softness. In fact, despite its lack of cushioning, I still found this to be one of the most comfortable.

Beyond the seat comfort, I was impressed by the sturdiness of the frame. It’s made of alloy steel and held up against scratches, heavier body weights, and exposure to sun and water. I also appreciated its locking mechanism; it’s essentially a handle on the back of the chair that snaps the frame in place and keeps the material taut. While it takes some effort to put into place, it allows you to shift around and even set it up on uneven ground without risk of it tipping while you lounge.

At more than 13 pounds, the Trailhead may be too heavy for some if there’s a long trek to camp. But its carrying case has backpack straps that are comfortable to wear, plus it keeps your arms free. Even on a walk of just around 10 to 15 minutes, I did feel its weight. It also isn’t cheap—it’s the most expensive camping chair we tested—and we wish it came in more than a couple colors, like Yeti’s impressive selection of coolers.

GCI has staked its claim as the king of camp comfort with its Rocker line of chairs. And the Kickback is Director of Product Content Will Egensteiner’s longtime favorite, keeping its spot on this list for close to six years now. Pistons on the back legs help with the rocking motion, and he found the resistance stiff enough that he wouldn’t accidentally tip the chair over backward—but not so aggressive that it felt like the Kickback was pitching him forward.

Both Egensteiner, who’s 6-foot-2, and another 5-foot-5 tester liked the seat height and had no problems sitting down and standing up. Egensteiner also liked that it has the usual cup holder and phone pocket on the armrests.

Despite that the chair is cumbersome to carry over a shoulder, the strap didn’t dig in. The Kickback is best for light activities such as car camping, backyard hangs, and picnics where you don’t have to lug it too far.

Some padding in the seat and backrest would be nice, but the fabric has some slack that makes the Kickback comfortable to sit in. Plus, the rocker design provides a nice recline that takes you off your knees and feet.

Full GCI Outdoor Kickback Rocker Camping Chair Review

What sets the Helinox Chair One (re) apart from others is how compactly it packs down. Like earlier generations, the newest version of this ultralight chair has tubing that disassembles similar to tent poles, so it fits inside a mid-size backpack with room to spare. Along with its economical size, it’s also the lightest chair we recommend by several pounds. That makes it a good choice for hikes and backpacking trips.

During testing, I hauled the chair in its carrying pouch for close to half a mile on mixed terrain. Unlike some other options I tested, the Chair One (re) caused no strain at all.

That said, most other chairs were also ready to go the second I got to my destination. This camping chair must be set up. I had to lock the frame poles in place and stretch the cover over four different holding points. This took less than five minutes, which isn't much time, but is certainly more than other models.

Despite the small size, I actually found the chair incredibly comfortable. The design naturally provides a bit of recline and I was able to relax in it with ease. The material also offered a bit of give on the sides, which molded to my body.

If a little extra comfort is a major priority, the REI Co-Op Westward padded camping chair is a great choice. The foldable chair has foam padding sewn into the polyester material that provides a slightly more forgiving feel as you sit down. This made a major difference for me as the seated hours began to add up. Instead of readjusting every 20 minutes or so, I was able to sink in comfortably and let the padding carry the extra weight.

That said, my absolute favorite feature on the chair is the cup holder. The cup holder is built underneath the seat and swivels out when needed. That means I get the full arm rest for my arms and my drink is still inches away. The cup holder itself is also quite large, wide enough to fit my 32-ounce water bottle.

Full REI Co-Op Westward Padded Chair Review

If portability is your biggest concern, the Crazy Creek AirCliner is the only camping chair we’ve tested and deflates, rolls up, and fits in a backpack with ease. The inflatable chair is also deceptively comfortable. In fact, once you find the sweet spot (which admittedly takes a minute), it genuinely rivals any other chair on this list.

Setup is also a breeze. After unclipping the latches and rolling out the chair, it takes just five full breaths to fully inflate it. One of the biggest concerns was that it would leak air over time, but after more than an hour of sitting, there was no noticeable softness or leakage.

The obvious downside is that there’s no frame, so you’ll be sitting right on the ground with your legs in front of you. While this isn’t a dealbreaker, it’s certainly something to consider

A camping chair’s durability is evaluated based on the frame, the material of the seat and back, and overall weather-resistance. Most of the camping chairs we write about are made with steel tubing that’s powder-coated or treated to resist rust and corrosion. This style of frame holds several hundred pounds without any bowing or bending and is still light enough to carry in your hands.

However, each chair on this list has a much different weight capacity so make sure to double check before you make your final purchase.

Similarly, seat durability relies on sturdy materials. Woven polyester is one of the most common options. Camping chair materials are often combined with a water-resistant coating so any spilled drinks or rain drops don't damage the fabric. This also protects any interior cushioning from absorbing water.

Great camping chairs are also treated to resist UV light. This helps prevent the fabric from fading over time. Similar to the metal frame, the fabric should also be strong enough to offer a weight capacity of 300 pounds at minimum.

While the most durable options (like the Yeti Trailhead) tend to be more expensive, think about upfront cost in relation to long-term use. If the chair lasts for several years, the initial cost is well worth it in comparison to a cheaper camping chair that might tear or break after just a couple of seasons.

Camping chairs are specifically designed to be portable. That said, the relative portability between them can range drastically.

Small, lightweight camping chairs pack down for easy transport and work well for backpackers or anyone traveling by foot. These typically come with carrying straps or collapse small enough to latch onto or pack into a large backpack. Ideally, they should weigh less than eight or nine pounds.

Larger chairs can weigh more than 10 pounds, which makes them far more cumbersome to carry and better suited to car camping and backyard lounging. What you get with that added size and weight, though, significantly more comfort afforded by a wider seat with more cushioning and a potentially higher weight limit.

Regardless of size, many camping chairs come with shoulder straps or carrying cases to make travel easier.

Camping chairs aren’t exclusively for camping, nor is all camping the same. If you simply want a chair for watching your kid’s soccer game or relaxing in the backyard, prioritize comfort above portability.

The more of an emphasis you put on comfort, the more added features are available to you. Many camping chairs come with foldout side tables, integrated cupholders, storage pouches, and even zip-up cooler bags.

For hikers and backpackers, smaller, lighter chairs are the obvious choices. If you’re using the chair for the beach, weather- and UV-resistance generally increase its longevity. It's also worth considering chairs with shorter legs so you can stretch out your own in the sand.

We carried the camping chairs through a park, taking note of how heavy they felt and whether they were cumbersome to transport up small hills and over boulders. After setting them up on grass and dirt patches to see how they balanced on uneven terrain, we took a seat, judging each by its relative comfort. Our testers spanned a range of heights and body weights so we could get a variety of impressions.

We have cumulative years with some chairs—including the Kelty Deluxe Lounge Chair and GCI Outdoor Kickback Rocker. And they still rank among the best. In subsequent updates, we’ve added several new camping chairs, including the Yeti Trailhead Field Chair and the Crazy Creek AirCliner. We evaluated each on its weight, stability, comfort, ease of setup, and durability.

Every chair on this list is one that we have personally tested over the past several years, so you can trust that each choice is based on real experience. We also made sure to keep price in mind.

#6346. NASA captures two powerful Pacific storms with a surprising connection

NASA satellites captured a rare super typhoon with an enormous eye as another powerful Pacific storm transformed and moved toward Alaska.

In late October 2026, two powerful storms dominated opposite ends of the North Pacific Ocean.

One developed an enormous, nearly circular eye, while the other transformed into a sprawling weather system that swept toward Alaska.

Yet both began as tropical cyclones in the western Pacific, and both appeared in a remarkable satellite view captured by NASA on October 29, 2026.

Super Typhoon In-fa was still an intense tropical system near the Mariana Islands.

Far to the north, the remnants of Typhoon Champi had transformed into an entirely different kind of storm.

Together, they offered a striking demonstration of how dramatically storms can change as they travel across the planet.

Super Typhoon In-fa stood out for its unusual structure.

NASA’s Terra satellite captured a closer view on October 30, revealing a remarkably symmetrical storm just west of the Mariana Islands.

In-fa displayed characteristics of an annular typhoon, a rare type of tropical cyclone with a distinctive ring-shaped structure.

Most typhoons develop long, spiraling bands of thunderstorms that extend outward from their centers.

Annular storms typically have fewer prominent outer rainbands, giving them a smoother, more circular appearance.

Their unusual structure has earned them comparisons to doughnuts and truck tires.

Only about four percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific develop annular characteristics.

These storms also tend to have larger eyes. While the eye of a typical tropical cyclone averages around 15 miles across, annular storms average nearly 30 miles.

Their structure can also help them maintain their strength longer when environmental conditions become less favorable.

While In-fa maintained its tropical identity, Champi was undergoing a dramatic transformation thousands of miles away.

Earlier in its journey, Champi had become one of the most powerful typhoons of 2026, with sustained winds approaching 185 miles per hour.

The storm brought damaging winds and heavy rainfall to several western Pacific locations, including Taiwan, Guam, China, and Japan.

But tropical cyclones depend on warm ocean water for energy. As Champi traveled northward, it encountered conditions that fundamentally changed how the storm operated.

Through a process known as extratropical transition, Champi’s remnants became incorporated into a larger weather system over the Bering Sea.

Instead of drawing energy primarily from warm ocean waters, the developing system was driven by temperature differences between air masses.

The change also transformed its appearance.

Tropical cyclones are generally organized around a central core, with powerful thunderstorms circling the eye.

Extratropical storms often look quite different from space. Their clouds can spread across enormous areas, forming sweeping bands that resemble giant commas.

These storms can also develop weather fronts, where contrasting air masses meet.

One particularly important change involves the area covered by strong winds.

NASA meteorologist Gary Partyka explained that a transitioning storm does not necessarily develop faster winds. Instead, its wind field can expand dramatically.

This means a storm can affect a much larger region even as its original tropical structure disappears.

Champi’s remnants became intertwined with an existing midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, likely helping intensify the larger weather system.

The resulting weather brought strong winds, heavy rainfall, and snow to parts of Alaska.

Alaska might seem an unlikely destination for a storm that began in the tropical Pacific, but the connection is well established.

Former typhoons sometimes travel northward and become part of the large weather systems that move across the North Pacific.

Champi was already the fourth former typhoon to reach Alaskan waters in 2026.

The others were Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October.

University of Alaska Fairbanks climatologist Rick Thoman noted that even the exceptionally strong El Niño years of 1997 and 2015 each brought only three former typhoons into the region during autumn.

Approximately 60 former typhoons have affected Alaska since 1970.

The unusually busy 2026 season raised questions about the broader atmospheric conditions helping steer these storms northward.

One possible contributor was the strong El Niño underway in the Pacific.

El Niño develops when surface waters across parts of the equatorial Pacific become warmer than usual, altering weather patterns across distant regions.

In the Northwest Pacific, these changes can influence where tropical cyclones form and how they travel.

Rather than moving steadily westward toward Asia, some storms are more likely to curve northward.

That shift can bring tropical cyclones closer to Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula.

It can also increase the opportunities for former typhoons to reach higher latitudes and interact with powerful northern storm systems.

El Niño is not responsible for every individual storm, but its influence on atmospheric circulation may help explain why the Pacific experienced such an active period.

The 2026 Northwest Pacific season had already produced more than two dozen named storms by late October.

In-fa was the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands that year, while Champi added to an unusually long list of former tropical cyclones reaching Alaska.

NASA’s satellite imagery captured an extraordinary contrast between two powerful storms, revealing how tropical cyclones can evolve as they move across different parts of the Pacific.

While In-fa retained its remarkable circular structure, Champi had become part of a much larger weather system.

Together, the storms offered a striking glimpse into the powerful atmospheric forces shaping weather across the Pacific.

Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using DSCOVR EPIC and MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

#6343. Cutting more trees could actually help forests store more carbon

A new study suggests that carefully managed tree harvesting could increase long-term carbon storage by reducing tree deaths and preserving carbon in wood products.

The surest way to keep carbon in a forest seems obvious: stop cutting it.

Trees left standing continue growing and storing carbon. But as forests age, growth can slow and more trees die, gradually releasing their stored carbon.

Researchers who modeled every forest in China project that cutting more trees, earlier and in the right places, would store more carbon by 2100 than today’s restrictions do.

But the calculation only works when carbon stored in harvested wood products is included.

The gain is a calculation, not a measurement. It depends on the harvested wood being turned into products that last, and it comes from a model run under a single climate model.

Zhen Yu of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology and Shirong Liu of the Chinese Academy of Forestry led the work, with co-authors at the U.S. Forest Service, the University of Exeter and CREAF in Spain.

The authors wrote that their findings challenge a widely held assumption: cutting the least always stores the most.

China swung from heavy logging to strict protection in the late 1980s, and its forest area has grown ever since.

Over the same years, its wood consumption rose more than tenfold, to 0.534 billion cubic meters in 2020, and more than 40% of that wood is imported.

The country now buys more wood from abroad than any other.

The authors drew on 15.5 million tree measurements from 415,000 inventory plots surveyed between 1999 and 2018.

Harvests got lighter over that period: more plots were cut, but the volume taken per cut fell by nearly half. Meanwhile the number of plots with dying trees kept rising.

Between the sixth and ninth national inventories, harvested volume dropped 46% while the volume lost to tree death rose 24%.

The pattern was strongest in old stands, which lost roughly four to five times as much wood to death as younger forests did.

China sorts its forests into timber forests, protection forests kept for soil, water and wildlife, and multifunctional reserves where commercial logging is excluded.

The reserves held 23% more standing wood per hectare than the timber forests, and their tree deaths rose 53% between 1999 and 2018.

The team ran two futures through an ecosystem model it first checked against the inventory record from 1980 to 2018. One continued current practice.

The other adjusted how much timber to harvest, when to harvest it, and where to cut based on forest age and type.

It opened suitable reserves to regulated harvesting and left protected areas and fragile ground alone.

Under current practice, the model projects that wood lost to tree death would climb to 0.43 billion cubic meters a year by 2100.

Dead trees amounted to about 71% of the timber harvest in 2020, and the authors estimate that by 2100 they would exceed it. More wood would rot than would be cut.

The adjusted plan harvests some stands before their trees die.

The model estimates it would cut mortality losses by 1.82 billion cubic meters (64 billion cubic feet) between 2020 and 2100, a 6.7% reduction.

Timber output would rise from 0.32 billion to 0.44 billion cubic meters a year, a 38% increase.

The extra timber would cut China’s reliance on imports, the authors wrote.

They calculated that the country’s wood self-sufficiency would rise from 59% to 81% under the plan. Domestic production met 46% of demand in 2023.

More cutting leaves less carbon in living trees, and the model shows that. By 2100 the standing stock under the adjusted plan is 2.41 billion cubic meters lower than under current practice.

Counting the carbon held in harvested wood products changes the sum.

Assuming wood use remains at 2020 levels, the model projects 4.2% more total carbon storage under the adjusted plan, equivalent to an additional 520 million metric tons of carbon.

The team’s supplementary accounting puts the climate benefit at roughly 550 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually.

None of this is a case for indiscriminate logging. The modeled benefit depends on forest age, ecological limits, and what happens to the wood after it leaves the forest.

The researchers didn’t track soil carbon, which can rise or fall after harvesting.

Their model moves a dead tree’s carbon straight into the soil pool, skipping the years or decades a standing dead trunk can hold carbon.

And every future ran under one climate model across four emissions pathways. The authors wrote that the difference between the two plans is therefore more trustworthy than either plan’s absolute numbers.

The 4.2% figure also rests on wood products being used the way they were in 2020.

How much of a harvested log becomes a beam that lasts 50 years, rather than paper or fuel, is a market question the forest model can’t answer.

The aging-forest problem is not China’s alone, the authors wrote. Europe and North America face the same mix of older stands, rising disturbance and growing demand for wood.

Whether carefully managed harvesting could deliver similar carbon benefits elsewhere remains an open question.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

#6341. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

#6340. The happiness curve has changed, and young adults are struggling most

A global study of nearly 54,000 adults reveals a troubling shift in happiness, with young people reporting the lowest levels of well-being.

For decades, research suggested that happiness reaches its lowest point in middle age, with people feeling better in their younger and later years.

Researchers surveying adults around the world have now found little sign of that midlife dip.

Young adults reported the lowest well-being of any age group, and scores rose fairly steadily from there with age. The researchers call the pattern alarming, and wealthy countries were not spared.

Kai Ruggeri, a professor of health policy and management at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, led the work.

His team of 261 researchers, all of whom took part as volunteers, surveyed nearly 54,000 adults in 92 countries.

Most people answered online and chose to take part, so the results describe the people who responded rather than whole nations. The authors make that point again and again.

“These findings are more than just a sign to policymakers that solutions are necessary to improve mental health among young people or those struggling to make ends meet,” Ruggeri said.

“In fact, they are a flashing red light that entire populations are already struggling and feel their resilience is diminished here and now, not only a concern for an uncertain future.”

Each participant rated ten statements about their own life. The scale ran from 1, meaning absolutely disagree, to 7, meaning absolutely agree.

The statements included “I feel full of energy,” “I feel calm and peaceful,” and “I recover quickly from things that go wrong in my life.”

Together, the statements measure different aspects of well-being, including optimism, resilience, and a sense of purpose.

The ten-part framework came from the well-being researcher Felicia Huppert and a colleague. Huppert died shortly before the work began, and the team dedicated the study to her.

She was told the day before her death that it would be carried out in her name.

Popular rankings such as the World Happiness Report rely on a few broad questions.

The authors wrote that two countries with the same life satisfaction score, say 7 out of 10, offer no clue about how either one could improve.

Samples from Denmark and Norway made the point. Both had an average life satisfaction of 6.2 out of 10, yet across the ten statements Denmark’s scores were spread more widely than Norway’s.

Participants also answered four standard screening questions about depression and anxiety over the previous two weeks.

People took the survey between June and August 2025, in 50 languages, and a typical participant finished in about six minutes.

People rated their relationships and their sense of meaning highest. On the 7-point scale, having support from people they’re close to averaged 5.05, and a sense of meaning averaged 4.93. Feeling full of energy came last, at 4.20.

Calm and the ability to recover from setbacks scored near the bottom too. The authors suggest those low scores fit with high rates of stress and burnout.

The difference was also clear among participants who gave the highest ratings of 6 or 7.

Just over 38% gave that answer about having support when they need it, but only 19.3% said the same about feeling full of energy.

The authors offer one possible reading of that gap. People may judge their own lives fairly kindly while feeling harmed by things they can’t control, such as unstable politics and economies.

Polls have described something similar, an optimism gap in which people feel better about their own lives than about society.

Only 6.5% of participants met a rough bar for flourishing. That meant scoring at least 60 out of a possible 70 on the ten statements while showing few signs of depression or anxiety.

The 38,133 participants who completed the screening questions showed the same age pattern.

Among people aged 18 to 25, only 14.7% showed no signs of depression or anxiety, compared with 23.6% of all participants.

At the other end, 28.6% of the young adults scored in the moderate to severe range, compared with 22.6% overall. Older groups did better, almost without exception.

Young adults in some wealthy countries fared worse still. In the UK sample, for example, only 6.1% showed no signs of depression or anxiety, while 42.8% scored moderate to severe.

The researchers’ first instinct was that their sample had produced the result. But a young and highly educated sample would typically skew results the other way, they wrote.

Other recent research has also found that younger adults now report the most distress.

Being free of depression and anxiety wasn’t the same as doing well, since many participants with no signs of either still scored low on the ten statements.

Well-being scores were higher at nearly every step up in household income, and the team found no clear point where the gains stopped.

That cuts against the common claim that money stops adding happiness past a certain income.

People who grew up in wealthier families scored higher as well.

Education followed a similar pattern. Each additional level of schooling was associated with higher average well-being.

The authors wrote that the education pattern contradicts claims that a university degree has lost its value.

People without paid work, whatever the reason, scored lower than workers, students, and retirees.

“Leaders can no longer use vague platitudes that hand-wave toward investing in non-specific mental health initiatives,” Ruggeri said.

Instead, he said, leaders need to make specific commitments.

Those include protecting livelihoods against job losses driven by AI, tackling burnout in young and working-age people, and improving access to care for mental illness.

People who lived with more family members or housemates generally reported higher levels of well-being than those living alone. Living alone was particularly common among older adults.

Among participants aged 75 and older, 44.9% lived by themselves, compared with 27.1% of all participants.

Among workers, people who split their time about evenly between home and the workplace scored highest, at 48.2 on a scale running from 10 to 70.

Those who worked entirely from home or entirely on site scored lowest, at 46.3 and 46.6.

The gaps between work arrangements were small. The researchers also couldn’t tell whether hybrid work helps or whether jobs that offer it are simply better jobs to begin with.

People in military service, a small part of the sample, scored highest of any work group.

The authors wrote that this likely reflects the relationships, energy, and sense of purpose common in a military unit.

Men scored slightly higher than women, though the difference was extremely small.

Everyone answered once, so the survey shows links rather than causes. The samples were uneven too, and in Chad almost everyone who took part was an academic.

Ruggeri’s team warned against ranking countries, because the statements may not mean exactly the same thing in every language.

A low average for Sweden, they wrote, doesn’t mean an employed, well-educated Swede is worse off than an unemployed person with little schooling in Uzbekistan.

Young people with unaddressed worries may have been eager to take part, and the oldest participants may have been unusually connected and energetic.

The authors wrote that those effects alone can’t explain a pattern this large.

Why young adults scored so low remains open. The authors raised two possibilities they didn’t test, starting with a steady stream of messages about stress, conflict, and lack of opportunity.

The other is loneliness, since young adults meet people in person less often than in the past, according to an OECD report.

Ruggeri’s team plans deeper analyses of wealth and well-being and calls for local studies within countries. In the authors’ view, those studies can best show governments which changes would help.

The full study was published in the journal Social Indicators Research.

#6339. Astronomers discover a ghostly green star that shouldn’t exist

Astronomers have identified a ghostly green white dwarf, along with dead stars that appear pink, purple, yellow, and cyan, challenging expectations about stellar colors.

Stars typically glow in shades of red, orange, white, or blue, with their colors revealing their temperatures. Even burned-out stars, known as white dwarfs, were thought to follow this rule.

But astronomers have discovered something extraordinary: a dead star that would appear green to the human eye.

The unusual color comes from sodium in the star’s atmosphere, which absorbs orange light and leaves behind a ghostly green glow.

Astronomers say no green star of any kind has ever been credibly reported.

The team’s research also revealed white dwarfs that would appear pink, purple, yellow, and cyan, with each unusual color linked to the chemical makeup of the star’s atmosphere.

Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the University of Warwick, led the work.

Boris Gänsicke and Pier-Emmanuel Tremblay at Warwick, along with Detlev Koester at Kiel University in Germany, were his co-authors.

No white dwarf is close enough for its color to be seen directly. Instead, astronomers calculate the color from the star’s light, and the green star’s measurement is a noisy one.

A white dwarf is what’s left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel and its core is all that remains. The coolest ones have atmospheres about as dense as water, and that density is the key.

Like a piece of iron heated to increasingly high temperatures, ordinary stars glow red, orange, or white depending on how hot they are.

Bright stars like Betelgeuse look redder than their neighbors, but they stay inside that range.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs,” Hollands said.

In an atmosphere that dense, a trace of carbon, calcium, or sodium absorbs light across a wider band of colors than it would in a thin gas.

That absorption can give a star colors that its temperature alone cannot explain.

A star’s spectrum is its light split by wavelength, the way a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow. Astronomers record spectra routinely.

The team ran spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and from their own atmosphere models through a mathematical description of human color vision that dates from 1931.

Each spectrum came out as the color a computer screen would need to show it.

The one thing a screen can’t show is brightness, because a real star’s surface is millions of times brighter than any monitor.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hollands said the calculation is more direct than a photograph would be.

Research telescopes record light through filters chosen for science rather than to match the eye, so their color images are false color.

A consumer camera on a research telescope could in principle show the same colors the team calculated, he said, but the spectrum already holds all of the star’s visible light.

“So this is the most accurate way to determine these colors short of actually going to visit these stars, which sadly won’t be happening at any time soon!” Hollands said.

The green star is WD J1330+6435, with a surface at about 7,200°F (4,000°C). Its helium atmosphere carries calcium, lithium, and sodium.

Those are the leftovers of asteroids or comets from its own planetary system, the same kind of debris seen falling onto other dead stars.

“The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow,” Hollands said.

Calcium removes the violet as well, so the light that remains peaks near 500 nanometers. In the team’s model the star comes out chartreuse, which is a yellowish green.

Of all the unusual colors revealed by the research, one stood out to Hollands more than any other: the chartreuse green of WD J1330+6435.

“Green is generally considered an implausible colour for a star to have,” Hollands told Earth.com.

What would the sky look like from a planet around the star?

On an Earth-like world it would probably still be pale blue, in a slightly different shade, Hollands said. The star’s green would show up on you instead.

“If you were wearing a white shirt (or space-suit), then you would see your outfit illuminated the pale green color that we determined from its spectrum,” he said.

Two other white dwarfs in the sample came out a much paler green.

A cousin of the green star, WD J2356-2054, carries so much sodium that almost no light escapes from the middle of the spectrum.

At the same temperature, it comes out a vivid blue.

At the other extreme is WD J1011+2845, just 48 light-years away, with a surface near 7,300°F (4,000°C).

Movement within the star has carried carbon from its interior to the surface. There, the carbon forms molecules that absorb most of the blue, green, and yellow light.

Almost all of its visible light comes out beyond 600 nanometers, at the red end, and the result is a deep, salmon pink.

The team called it likely the reddest star known in terms of perceived color.

Among 36 carbon-rich white dwarfs the team examined, the cooler ones mostly came out in shades of pink.

Stars like it are hard to model, and a strong magnetic field may be distorting this one’s light in ways that the models don’t fully capture.

Hydrogen can tint a cool white dwarf as well, Hollands said. A trace of it forms H2 molecules, and their collisions with the dense helium can leave the star looking cyan or turquoise.

To find out how common the oddities are, the team took every white dwarf within 65 light-years (20 parsecs) of the Sun, 152 stars in all.

Five had colors too far from a heated-iron glow to be assigned a temperature: two yellow and three pink.

Five of 152 is about 3.4 percent, or roughly one in 30. For the rest, the team measured the color temperature, the scale printed on light bulb boxes, where 3,000 kelvin is warm white and 6,000 is cool white.

The median came out just under 6,800 kelvin, which the eye sees as white.

Gänsicke said the result corrects a habit.

“One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there,” he said.

White dwarfs are usually drawn blue because the hot, blue ones are the brightest and show up most often in surveys. The nearby sample has no such bias. Within it, 95 percent of the stars fall between 3,800 and 18,700 kelvin.

The green star and the blue one are the same kind of object with different amounts of sodium.

The team therefore expects to find other white dwarfs with colors ranging from green to cyan and blue.

No other star quite like the green one is known yet, Hollands emphasized.

“Right now there are multiple spectroscopic surveys coming online which will be taking spectra of hundreds of thousands of white dwarfs, so hopefully we’ll find a few more, perhaps even more vivid green examples,” Hollands told Earth.com.

No white dwarf is bright enough to see without a telescope, but the team has developed a way to create color-accurate images of these stars.

As new surveys examine hundreds of thousands of white dwarfs, astronomers may soon discover even more unexpected colors hiding among the stars.

The full study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

#6336. Tiny ocean buoys could transform how we predict powerful storms

Scientists found that drifting weather buoys in the Mediterranean Sea helped improve forecasts during a powerful storm that battered Sicily.

Modern weather forecasting relies heavily on satellites watching the planet around the clock.

Yet, when storm Harry drowned parts of Sicily in rain this January, a handful of barometers bobbing in the Ionian Sea helped the forecast.

Until the previous fall, that patch of sea had almost no weather instruments at the surface. Scientists dropped the barometer buoys there on purpose.

A project called the Mediterranean Extreme Events Experiment, or M3E, began releasing them in September 2025 to fill a long-standing observation gap. Storm Harry was its first big test.

A team led by David Lavers of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts found that the buoys’ pressure readings reduced forecast error during the storm.

“The Mediterranean is a relatively small sea, but it can generate very powerful storms, and the countries around it pay a high price,” said Emanuela Clementi, a senior scientist at the CMCC Foundation in Bologna and a co-author of the study.

“With M3E we are filling a gap in the observations precisely where these storms form. Storm Harry gave us the first evidence that these data help forecasts,” she added.

Every forecast starts from a snapshot of the atmosphere. That snapshot comes from millions of measurements a day, from satellites, aircraft, balloons and ground stations.

But thick clouds and heavy rain blur what a satellite sees in the lower atmosphere. So a barometer at the surface in the right place still carries unusual weight.

Yet surface weather instruments have long been scarce across the Ionian Sea and central Mediterranean.

The region has seen extreme storms since biblical times, the authors wrote, and persistent cyclones tend to form there.

Three recent ones, storm Apollo in 2021, storm Daniel in 2023 and now Harry, did heavy damage around the basin.

The barometer buoys that filled the gap drift with the current. An underwater drogue hanging 49 feet (15 meters) below each one keeps it from washing ashore too quickly.

Fifteen came from the Global Drifter Program at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, and five more were paid for by Italy’s OGS oceanography institute.

Each buoy measures air pressure and sea surface temperature, relays the numbers by satellite every hour, and feeds them into the global weather data stream within minutes.

The first seven went into the Ionian Sea in early September 2025, five from the research vessel Laura Bassi and two from a passing container ship.

More followed through February 2026. By late March, 10 of the 20 were still working; the rest had run aground in southern Italy or Greece, or been picked up by sailors.

One buoy drifted out of the Ionian Sea into the Adriatic and ended up along its eastern shore, tracing the regional current as it went.

Storm Harry formed as a small low over Morocco and deepened over Algeria a day later. Then it stalled over Tunisia and the central Mediterranean for days.

A steady southeasterly wind built waves of about 26 feet (8 meters) and drove moist air into the mountains of Sardinia, Sicily and Calabria.

Between January 19 and 21, 23 weather stations recorded more than 11.8 inches (300 millimeters) of rain. Eight of them passed 15.7 inches (400 millimeters), and eastern Sicily recorded the highest total, 19 inches (482.5 millimeters).

The toll was heavy. Losses in Sicily alone were estimated at more than €1 billion, a landslide hit the town of Niscemi, and people died in North Africa.

The European forecast model saw the Sicilian deluge coming about seven days ahead, helped by mountains like Mount Etna, which force moist air upward in the same place every time.

Northern Tunisia fared worse. One station there recorded 8.1 inches (207 millimeters), while the forecast issued at the start of January 19 had a median of just 1.6 inches (41.4 millimeters).

The authors suspect four small low-pressure systems between the Balearic Islands and North Africa contributed to the forecasting difficulties. Such systems are difficult to predict far in advance.

The team used two tests. The first scores every observation on whether it made the next day’s forecast better or worse.

Throughout the winter, the buoys’ scores were small but mostly positive, as expected when forecasts are already accurate.

On January 19, as Harry crossed the Ionian Sea, pressure at one buoy dropped sharply. Its readings proved particularly helpful in improving the forecast.

In the second test, the team reran the forecast for the storm’s two peak days with every drifting barometer buoy in the Mediterranean removed.

Near the Balearic Islands, where those four small lows sat, the two versions differed by about 2 hectopascals of pressure.

That pressure difference may seem small, but it can matter when forecasting compact weather systems.

The small lows were sensitive to pressure readings taken hundreds of miles to the east.

“These systems highlight the importance of collecting observations directly at sea,” Clementi said.

“The Ionian Sea and central Mediterranean have historically had limited coverage of in-situ atmospheric measurements, despite being areas where intense storms and persistent cyclones can develop.”

The authors call this a preliminary assessment. It rests on a single storm and a two-day rerun.

Four buoys received slightly negative scores after being deployed during relatively calm weather in late February, when their readings offered little opportunity to improve the forecasts.

The buoys are also a tiny fraction of everything the model takes in.

The team expects each one to count for more than a reading from a well-covered area, because it fills a gap.

Whether more buoys could help prevent forecasting errors like those seen in Tunisia remains uncertain.

The researchers now plan to focus on the small low-pressure systems that contributed to those errors.

Another 20 to 30 buoys are due to go into the Ionian and Tyrrhenian Seas starting this fall. The next Mediterranean storm will meet far more eyes at the surface.

The full study was published in the journal Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society.

#6335. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6334. Sun Joe Electric Wood Chipper Review: Turn That Storm Cleanup Into Usable Mulch

This light-duty wood chipper is ideally suited and priced for the average yard.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

My backyard runs up to a wooded area. Although there are few trees on my actual property, any storm that comes through pushes twigs and branches from the wooded area onto my lawn. And with several large rose bushes to tend to, I have a fair amount of clippings to break down. Gathering this debris up in a large waste container has been my approach for cleaning up my yard. But leaving this debris on the curb to be hauled off to the local landfill or burning it in my fire pit seemed like a waste, especially since I have landscaping beds and a garden that could benefit from this yard waste.

Purchasing a gas-powered wood chipper to break this waste down into usable mulch felt like overkill. Plus, I didn’t have space to store a gas chipper, nor did I want to fork over $600 or $700 for one of these machines. Enter the Sun Joe CJ603E electric wood chipper.

It doesn’t have the wood-chipping power of a gas wood chipper like the Champion portable gas wood chipper or the Earthquake K32 wood chipper, but it does what I need it to do. It can chip small branches and twigs, and costs a fraction of a gas-powered wood chipper. Plus, it’s a manageable weight and size, so it’s easy to move around and store. I spent several months testing the Sun Joe for our Best Wood Chippers buying guide earlier this year and have been using it to assist with yard cleanup ever since. It’s proven to be up to the task.

What better way to test the Sun Joe CJ603E’s wood-chipping abilities than to feed it as many twigs and branches as possible? And since my property backs up to a densely wooded area, I had plenty of fodder for it to chew on. Keeping to its listed max branch diameter of 1.73 inches, I crammed dead, dry branches into the Sun Joe.

Along with its ability to chew up dead wood, I also wanted to see how it handled green material, so I used the CJ603E to break down clippings trimmed from several large rose bushes on my property. Lastly, I also considered how well the Sun Joe was able to chip material into bits that were small enough to serve as mulch.

The Sun Joe CJ603E is one of the easiest wood chippers I’ve tested. For starters, assembly took just a few minutes. It only weighs 38 pounds and sits on two wheels, so moving it from my garage to my backyard felt effortless compared to moving gas wood chippers that weigh well over 100 pounds. The Sun Joe CJ603E uses a standard wall outlet for power, so it requires an extension cord, which limits its range compared to a gas-powered model. That said, the CJ603E also starts at the push of a button, so there’s no wrestling with a pull starter. At about 3 feet tall assembled on its stand, the Sun Joe is roughly the size of a counter-height bar stool with a backrest. That’s much smaller than a full-size gas wood chipper, which is important for garages like mine that are strapped for space.

We at Popular Mechanics are already familiar with Sun Joe’s line of wood chippers, having tested an earlier model a few years ago. Sun Joe’s CJ603E is a clear upgrade. The addition of a pressure plate that forces branches and twigs up against the blades gives this updated model more cutting power than its predecessor. The results were noticeable during testing.

I began my testing with dried-out dead wood, beginning with smaller twigs before working up to larger branches. The Sun Joe handled it all well, even consuming branches that were pushing beyond its listed 1.73-inch-diameter capacity.

The CJ603E is a prolific eater. I was able to feed sticks into it continuously without having to wait for the blades to chew through already-loaded material. And since the machine pulls sticks into it, there’s no need to use a separate stick to push material down its throat (though the CJ603E does include one).

The CJ603E does have an Achilles’ heel, and that’s with thicker, greener branches that exceed 1.5 inches in diameter. This “wet” wood had a tendency to clog the output chute, creating torn pieces rather than cleanly cut chips. While this wasn’t a huge issue for me, it could be for someone who uses a wood chipper to clean up live branches brought down during a storm.

Another benefit of the CJ603E is that it operates more quietly than the loud gas-powered models I’ve tested and does not produce exhaust, though you should still wear hearing protection when operating it. The CJ603E also requires far less maintenance since it doesn’t use a gas engine.

The Sun Joe CJ603E produces wood chips suitable for mulching, but don’t expect them to have a uniform look. Depending on what I was chipping, the CJ603E produced anywhere from 1/2-inch- to 1-inch-long wood chips, which was coarser than I expected given its listed 21:1 reduction ratio. I also noticed that the CJ603E would allow some longer twigs to pass through without being completely chopped. Since these irregularities make the wood chips less ideal for use in decorative landscaping, I use them as a base layer with a top layer of commercial mulch in my landscaping.

Sun Joe’s CJ603E wood chipper does what it’s designed for well. It can chip branches and twigs up to 1.73 inches in diameter into wood chips for easy disposal or use as mulch. Its compact size and comparatively light weight make it easy to move from garage or shed to yard and back again, and it doesn’t take up a huge amount of space in a shed or garage.

Homeowners will also appreciate the ease of use an electric wood chipper offers compared to gas models, since there’s no gas-powered engine to start or maintain. These factors, along with its low purchase cost, make it a smart option for homeowners looking for something that can handle modest yard cleanup.

That said, it’s important to understand that the Sun Joe CJ603E does not match the power of gas-powered wood chippers designed for residential use. Gas-powered wood chippers are more capable, with most able to chew through branches up to 3 inches in diameter. Their powerful engines also make them capable of moving through branches at a higher rate. There’s also a difference in durability. While the Sun Joe has numerous plastic parts, gas wood chippers have mainly metal construction, so they can better endure bigger jobs and more frequent use.

The Sun Joe is also a dedicated wood chipper. Unlike chipper/shredders, the CJ603E doesn’t have a shredder function that will reduce leaves into mulch. If you're looking for a wood chipper that can handle bigger branches and shred leaves, we suggest one of our other recommended models below.

This gas wood chipper chewed through 3-inch branches with ease when we tested it, and it also doubles as a very effective leaf shredder. Couple that performance with a reasonable price tag, and it’s an ideal gas wood chipper for homeowners with wooded lots to manage.

This is the most affordable gas wood chipper we could find that still has the chops to get the job done. It’s capable of grinding through branches up to 3 inches in diameter and has a chute that makes it easy to deposit those wood chips directly into your landscaping. It only chips wood, though. If you’re looking for something that can also shred leaves, you’ll need to look elsewhere.

Earthquake’s K32 wood chipper boasted some of the most impressive wood-chipping power we experienced of any of the models we tested. What’s more, it produces some of the smallest wood chips. If you’re looking for a machine to create high-quality mulch for your landscaping, then spring for this one.

#6333. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta
